rules.title: Some and any
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You need it to talk about amounts when ordering, shopping and asking for things.

**In simple words** — `some` in positive sentences: `I have some milk`. `any` in negatives and questions: `I don't have any milk`, `Do you have any?`

**The idea** — `Some` and `any` say that there is an amount or a number, without saying exactly how much. English chooses between them by the type of sentence: statement, negative or question.

**The form**
- Statements: `some` + plural or uncountable noun — `some apples`, `some milk`
- Negatives: `not ... any` — `don't have any money`
- Questions: `any` — `is there any`
- Offers and requests: `some`, because you expect "yes" — `would you like some`
- After `if`: `any` — `if you have any problems`
- `Never`, `hardly` and `without` are negative in meaning, so they take `any`
- Compounds follow the same pattern: `something`, `anything`, `someone`, `anyone`

**When it applies**
- An unknown or unimportant amount: `some`, `any`
- Signal words: `there is`, `there are`, `have got`, `would you like`, `can I have`
- In negatives with `not`, `never`, `no one`, `hardly`

**When it does NOT apply** — With an exact number or a singular countable noun, use the number or `a`. For a large amount use `a lot of`; for questions about amount use `how much` and `how many`. Test: negative or open question → `any`; positive statement, offer or request → `some`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `some` in a negative: learners copy the positive pattern
- Using `any` in a positive statement, because the question pattern is overgeneralised; it needs a negative or an open question
- Using `any` in an offer or request that expects "yes"
- Using `some` with a singular countable noun (`some book`) — use `a`
- Using `no` and `not` together

**Register and usage** — Same in speech and writing. Stressed `some` can mean "certain" (`some people think`), which is a different use.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `Any` in a positive sentence means "it does not matter which": `any day`
- `No` + noun is the same as `not any`

rules.title: Much, many and a lot of
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You use it every time you talk about amounts: food, money, time, people.

**In simple words** — `many` goes with things you can count (`many friends`), `much` with things you cannot (`much water`). `a lot of` works for both in positive sentences.

**The idea** — English asks first: can you count the thing? Countable nouns (`book`, `friend`) have plurals and numbers. Uncountable nouns (`water`, `money`, `time`, `information`) do not. The word for 'a large amount' depends on this.

**The form**
- `many` + plural countable noun: `many books`, `many people`
- `much` + uncountable noun: `much time`, `much money`
- `a lot of` / `lots of` + either type, mainly in positive sentences
- `much` and `many` are normal in negatives and questions: `not much`, `how many`, `how much`
- In positive sentences `much` is rare in speech; use `a lot of`
- Uncountable nouns have no plural and no `a`: `information`, `advice`, `furniture`, `homework`, `news`

**When it applies**
- Questions about amount: signal words `how much`, `how many`
- Negatives: `not much`, `not many`, `too much`, `too many`
- Positive statements with a large amount: `a lot of`, `lots of`

**When it does NOT apply** — For a small amount use `a few` (countable) or `a little` (uncountable); for a positive large amount in speech use `a lot of`. Test: if you can add `-s` or put a number before it, use `many`; if not, use `much`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `much` with plural nouns, or `many` with uncountables (`many time`, `much books`)
- Using `much` in positive sentences, where it sounds formal or odd
- Giving uncountable nouns a plural (`informations`, `furnitures`, `advices`)
- Using `a` with an uncountable noun

**Register and usage** — `a lot of` is neutral and the best default in positive sentences.
rules.llmDescription: Quantifiers much, many, a lot of and countability: much with plural nouns, many with uncountables, much in positive statements, plurals of uncountable nouns such as informations or furnitures.

rules.title: In, on and at for time
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You need it for every appointment, schedule and plan, so it is very frequent.

**In simple words** — `at` for exact times (`at 5`), `on` for days and dates (`on Monday`), `in` for months, years, seasons and parts of the day (`in May`, `in the morning`).

**The idea** — English uses three small words to place an event in time. They work like boxes of different sizes: `in` for long periods, `on` for days and dates, `at` for exact points.

**The form**
- `at` + clock time and points: `at 5 o'clock`, `at noon`, `at midnight`, `at night`, `at the weekend` (British)
- `on` + days and dates: `on Monday`, `on 5 May`, `on Christmas Day`, `on Friday morning`
- `in` + months, seasons, years, centuries: `in July`, `in winter`, `in 1998`, `in the 21st century`
- `in` + parts of the day: `in the morning`, `in the afternoon`, `in the evening`
- `in` + a period from now: `in two weeks`, `in an hour`
- No preposition before `next`, `last`, `this`, `every`, `today`, `tomorrow`, `yesterday`

**When it applies**
- Saying when something happens: signal words `when`, `what time`, `which day`
- Schedules, birthdays, appointments and habits

**When it does NOT apply** — For duration use `for` (`for two hours`), for a start point use `since`, and for an end point use `until` or `by`. Test: if you name a clock time use `at`; a day or date use `on`; a longer period use `in`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `at` for days or months, or `in` for clock time, because one word is chosen for all time phrases
- Using `on` before months and years
- Using `in` for `night` (`in night`) and `on` for `the morning`
- Adding a preposition before `next` or `last`

**Register and usage** — `at the weekend` is British; American English says `on the weekend`.
rules.llmDescription: Time prepositions in, on, at: at with clock times and night, on with days and dates, in with months, years, seasons, parts of the day; added preposition before next, last.

examples.correct: My class starts at 9 o'clock.

rules.title: Because and so
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You use it all the time to explain and justify things.

**In simple words** — `because` gives the reason: `I'm tired because I worked late`. `so` gives the result: `I worked late, so I'm tired`.

**The idea** — `because` and `so` link the same two facts from opposite sides. `because` introduces the reason; `so` introduces the result. If you mix them, the cause and the effect change places and the meaning is wrong.

**The form**
- result + `because` + subject + verb: the reason follows
- `Because` + subject + verb + comma + result: the reason comes first
- reason + comma + `so` + subject + verb: the result follows
- `because` and `so` never appear together in one sentence
- a `because` clause has its own subject and verb
- before a noun phrase use `because of` + noun instead
- negative and question forms follow the normal clause: the conjunction does not change
- in the answer to `Why ...?`, start with `Because`

**When it applies**
- Giving a reason: `because`, answers to `why`
- Giving a result or consequence: `so`
- Explaining a choice or a feeling

**When it does NOT apply** — `because of` is used with a noun, not a clause. Test: after the word, is there a subject and a verb? Use `because`. Is there only a noun? Use `because of`. To decide between `because` and `so`, ask: is this the cause or the effect?

**Typical mistakes**
- Swapping the two: the learner puts the result after `because`; ask "which one happened first or caused the other?"
- Writing `because` and `so` together: one of them is enough
- Using `because` before a noun: use `because of`
- Writing a `because` clause alone as a full sentence: attach it to the main clause
- Putting a comma before `because` in a short sentence: usually not needed

**Register and usage** — Both are neutral. In speech `because` is often short (cos); in writing keep the full form.
rules.llmDescription: Because (reason, clause), because of (noun), so (result); errors are swapped roles, because with so together, because before a noun, because clause alone.

examples.wrong: I stayed home so it was raining.
examples.correct: I stayed home because it was raining.
examples.note: The reason needs because, not so.

examples.wrong: Because it was late, so we left.
examples.correct: Because it was late, we left.
examples.note: Do not use so after a because clause.

examples.wrong: She is happy because of she passed.
examples.correct: She is happy because she passed.
examples.note: Because of takes a noun, not a clause.

examples.wrong: He was ill, because he didn't come.
examples.correct: He was ill, so he didn't come.
examples.note: The result needs so, not because.

examples.correct: She was hungry so she ate a big lunch.
examples.note: The result needs so, not because.

examples.correct: My brother is tired because he worked late.
examples.note: A full clause needs because, not because of.

rules.title: No article with general nouns
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You need it every time you speak about likes, opinions and general facts.

**In simple words** — When you speak about things in general, use no article: `Dogs are friendly`, `I like music`. Use `the` only for a specific one: `the dog next door`.

**The idea** — When you talk about a whole group or a whole substance in general, English uses no article at all. The article `the` points to one particular thing that both speakers know; when you speak in general, there is nothing particular to point to.

**The form**
- plural noun alone: general meaning about all of them
- uncountable noun alone: general meaning about the whole substance or idea
- no `a` or `an` with plural nouns, because `a` means one
- no `a` or `an` with uncountable nouns
- no `the` before the noun when the meaning is general
- `the` appears only when the noun is limited: by a phrase, by context, or because it was mentioned before

**When it applies**
- Likes, dislikes and habits: after `like`, `love`, `hate`, `enjoy`
- General facts and truths about people, animals, things
- Abstract ideas: life, love, time, music, health
- Professions and groups seen as a class: signal is no specific place or moment

**When it does NOT apply** — Use `the` when both people know which one you mean. Test: can you ask "which ones?" If the answer is a particular group (the ones we saw, the ones in this room), use `the`; if it is all of them, use no article.

**Typical mistakes**
- Adding `the` to a general plural: the learner thinks a noun always needs a small word before it
- Adding `the` to uncountable nouns such as music, water, advice
- Adding `a` to a plural noun

**Register and usage** — This is standard in all registers. Newspaper headlines also drop articles.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- A bare noun can be specific when a following phrase limits it; then `the` returns
- Some abstract nouns take `the` only in a fixed phrase
rules.llmDescription: No article before general plural or uncountable nouns (music, children, coffee, life); errors are the or a added in a general meaning, a before a plural.

examples.note: Do not use the for general ideas.

examples.correct: We don't eat meat in my family.
examples.note: Meat in general needs no article.

rules.title: Few, a few, little and a little
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — It lets you describe small amounts and show if you see them as enough or too little.

**In simple words** — `a few` + countable (`a few friends`) and `a little` + uncountable (`a little time`) mean "some". `few` and `little` without `a` mean "almost none".

**The idea** — These words say that a number or an amount is small. The small word `a` changes the feeling: with `a` the speaker sees something positive (there is some); without `a` the speaker sees something negative (there is almost none). And English splits the words by noun type: one pair for things you count, one pair for things you cannot count.

**The form**
- `a few` + plural countable noun: some, enough
- `few` + plural countable noun: almost none, not enough
- `a little` + uncountable noun: some, enough
- `little` + uncountable noun: almost none, not enough
- the noun after `few` and `a few` is always plural
- the noun after `little` and `a little` is singular and has no ending
- negative: `not many` or `not much` is more common than `few` or `little` in speech
- question: use `many` and `much`, not these words, in most questions

**When it applies**
- Small numbers of countable things: friends, books, chairs, ideas
- Small amounts of uncountable things: money, time, water, sugar, hope
- Signal words: `only`, `quite`, `very`, `so`, `too` often go with `few` and `little`

**When it does NOT apply** — `much` and `many` express a large quantity; `some` is neutral. Test: can you count the noun? If yes, use `few`; if no, use `little`. Then ask: is it enough, or almost nothing? With `a` it is enough; without `a` it is almost nothing.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the pair for the wrong noun: `a few` with money, `a little` with friends
- Dropping `a`: this changes the meaning from some to almost none
- Adding a plural ending after `little`
- Using `a little` with a plural noun

**Register and usage** — Without `a`, `few` and `little` sound a little formal and negative. In everyday speech people say `not many` and `not much`.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `a little` can also be an adverb: a little tired
rules.llmDescription: Few, a few with countable plurals; little, a little with uncountables; a makes it positive; errors are the wrong pair for the noun, dropped or added a.

examples.correct: I have a little money for the bus.

examples.note: Birds are countable, so use a few.

rules.title: Adverbs of manner with -ly
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — It lets you say how people do things, not only what they do.

**In simple words** — To say how an action is done, usually add `-ly` to the adjective: `slow → slowly`. `She speaks quietly`, not "speaks quiet". Exception: `good → well`.

**The idea** — An adverb of manner tells us how an action is done. English builds most of them from an adjective by adding `-ly`. The adjective describes a noun; the adverb describes a verb. If you use the adjective after a verb, the sentence is wrong.

**The form**
- adjective + `-ly`: slow becomes slowly, quick becomes quickly
- adjective ending in `-y`: change `y` to `i`, then add `-ly`: happy becomes happily
- adjective ending in `-le`: drop `e`, add `-y`: simple becomes simply
- adjective ending in `-ic`: add `-ally`: basic becomes basically
- adjective ending in `-ful`: add `-ly`: careful becomes carefully (note the double l)
- position: after the verb, or after the object, never between the verb and its object
- position: before the verb is possible for some adverbs in writing
- negative and question forms do not change the adverb

**When it applies**
- After action verbs: speak, drive, walk, write, answer, sing
- Answers to the question `how?`

**When it does NOT apply** — After linking verbs such as `be`, `look`, `feel`, `seem`, `sound` use the adjective. Test: does the word describe the person or thing (adjective) or the action (adverb)?

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the adjective after an action verb: the learner copies the adjective form
- Putting the adverb between the verb and its object
- Spelling errors: `y` not changed to `i`, or only one `l` in `-fully`
- Adding `-ly` to irregular adverbs such as fast and hard

**Register and usage** — Neutral. Adverbs of manner are common in speech and writing.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `fast`, `hard`, `late` and `early` have the same form as adjectives
- `good` has the adverb `well`
rules.llmDescription: Manner adverbs with -ly (slowly, carefully, happily) after action verbs; errors are bare adjective after a verb, adverb before the object, wrong -ly spelling.

examples.correct: She speaks slowly.
examples.note: A verb needs an adverb with -ly.

examples.correct: He drives carefully.
examples.note: Use the adverb form after the verb.

examples.correct: We waited patiently for an hour.

examples.correct: She answered the question easily.

examples.correct: He shouted angrily at us.

examples.correct: She completed the form carefully and neatly.

rules.title: Should for advice
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You use it to give and ask for advice in friendly and work talk.

**In simple words** — `should` + plain verb: `You should rest`. Negative: `shouldn't`. It is a soft suggestion, not an order.

**The idea** — `should` is a soft way to give advice or say what is a good idea. It is not an order. It belongs to the small group of modal verbs, which add meaning to another verb and have a very simple form.

**The form**
- subject + `should` + base verb (the verb without `to`)
- `should` is the same for every person: I, you, he, she, it, we, they
- no `-s` ending in the third person singular
- negative: `should not` or `shouldn't` + base verb
- question: `Should` + subject + base verb
- question word: question word + `should` + subject + base verb
- short answer: `Yes, you should.` / `No, you shouldn't.`
- no `do` or `does` is used with `should`

**When it applies**
- Advice about health, study, work, everyday life
- Asking for advice: `What should I ...?`
- Saying what is a good or bad idea; signal words: `I think`, `I don't think`, `maybe`

**When it does NOT apply** — `must` and `have to` express strong duty or rules; `should` only suggests. Test: if the other person can say no without a problem, use `should`; if there is a rule or a real need, use `must` or `have to`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Adding `to` after `should`: the learner copies the pattern of ordinary verbs
- Adding `-s` to `should` after he, she or it
- Using `do` or `does` for questions and negatives
- Adding an ending or `-ing` to the verb after `should`
- Wrong word order in questions: the subject must come after `should`

**Register and usage** — Neutral, polite and very common. `ought to` is similar but less common.
rules.llmDescription: Should for advice: should + bare infinitive, same for all persons, shouldn't, inversion in questions; errors are should to, shoulds, do/does with should, -ing after should.

examples.correct: You should see a doctor.
examples.note: Do not use to after should.

examples.correct: He should drink more water.

examples.correct: Should I call her?

examples.correct: You shouldn't eat so much.

examples.correct: She should go to bed earlier.

examples.note: Do not use to after should not.

examples.correct: They should buy a new car.

examples.correct: What should I say to him?
examples.note: The subject follows should in questions.

examples.correct: Should your sister wait here?
examples.note: Do not use to after should.

rules.title: Can, could and may for requests
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — It helps you ask politely in shops, at work and when you travel.

**In simple words** — `Can you...?` is normal, `Could you...?` is more polite, `May I...?` is formal. `Could you open the window, please?`

**The idea** — To ask someone to do something, or to ask for permission, English uses modal verbs. `can` is the plain, everyday form; `could` is more polite; `may` is more formal and mostly used about yourself. The choice shows how polite you are.

**The form**
- `Can` / `Could` + you + base verb: asking someone to do something
- `Can` / `Could` / `May` + I + base verb: asking permission
- the verb after the modal has no `to`, no `-s` and no `-ing`
- the modal form does not change for I, you, he, she, it, we, they
- negative request: `Could you not ...` is rare; use `Please don't` instead
- polite word: `please` goes at the end or after the subject
- short answers: `Yes, of course.` / `Sure.` / `Sorry, I can't.`
- no `do` or `does` is used before these modals

**When it applies**
- Asking for help: `Can you ...?`, `Could you ...?`
- Asking permission: `Can I ...?`, `Could I ...?`, `May I ...?`
- Shops, offices, restaurants, the classroom; signal words: `please`, `excuse me`

**When it does NOT apply** — To give a command use the imperative; to offer help use `Shall I` or `Can I help`. Test: are you asking another person to do something (`you`), or asking to do something yourself (`I`)? `May you` is not used for requests.

**Typical mistakes**
- Adding `to` after the modal
- Adding `-ing` or `-s` to the verb after the modal
- Using `do you can` instead of `can you`
- Using `may` with `you` to ask for help: `may` is for `I` and `we`

**Register and usage**
- `Can` is neutral and common; `Could` is polite; `May` is formal and sounds careful.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `Could` in a request is not past time: it is just more polite
rules.llmDescription: Polite requests and permission: Can/Could you, Can/Could/May I + bare verb; errors are to or -ing after the modal, do you can, may you for requests.

examples.note: Do not use to after could.

examples.correct: Can he open the door for me?

examples.note: After may, use the base verb.

rules.title: The zero conditional
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You need it for facts, rules, instructions and general truths.

**In simple words** — `If` + present, present: for things that are always true. `If you heat ice, it melts`.

**The idea** — The zero conditional talks about things that are always true: facts, rules, habits and results that happen every time. The speaker is not guessing about a future moment. That is why both parts use the present simple.

**The form**
- `If` / `When` + subject + present simple, subject + present simple
- the `if` clause can come first, then a comma
- the `if` clause can come second, with no comma
- the present simple has the usual shape: base verb, with `-s` after he, she, it
- negative: `do not` / `does not` + base verb in either part
- question: `If ...?` is a clause; the main question uses `do` / `does`
- no `will` in the `if` clause or in the main clause
- no past tense in either clause for a present fact

**When it applies**
- Scientific and natural facts: water, heat, ice, plants
- Rules and instructions: machines, buttons, the school
- General habits and results; signal words: `always`, `usually`, `every time`, `whenever`

**When it does NOT apply** — The first conditional talks about one possible future event with `will`. Test: does the sentence describe something true every time (zero conditional), or one specific future situation (first conditional)?

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `will` in the `if` clause: the learner copies the future pattern
- Using the past in the main clause for a present fact
- Dropping the third person `-s`
- Wrong negative form: `not` before the verb without `do`
- Using `will` in the main clause when the fact is general

**Register and usage** — Neutral. `When` and `if` are interchangeable here, because the result is always the same.
rules.llmDescription: Zero conditional for general truths: if or when + present simple, present simple result; errors are will or past tense in either clause, missing -s, negation without do.

examples.wrong: If you heat ice, it melted.
examples.correct: If you heat ice, it melts.
examples.note: A general fact needs the present simple.

examples.wrong: If I will drink coffee late, I can't sleep.
examples.correct: If I drink coffee late, I can't sleep.
examples.note: Do not use will in the if clause.

examples.wrong: When water freezes, it became ice.
examples.correct: When water freezes, it becomes ice.
examples.note: A general result needs the present simple.

examples.wrong: If it rains, the streets are being wet.
examples.correct: If it rains, the streets are wet.
examples.note: Use the present simple, not the continuous.

examples.wrong: If people not eat, they get weak.
examples.correct: If people don't eat, they get weak.
examples.note: Negative present simple needs do not.

examples.wrong: If she is cold, she put on a coat.
examples.correct: If she is cold, she puts on a coat.

examples.wrong: If you press this button, the door opened.
examples.correct: If you press this button, the door opens.
examples.note: The result clause needs the present simple.

examples.wrong: Plants die if they will not get water.
examples.correct: Plants die if they do not get water.
examples.note: Do not use will in the if clause.

examples.wrong: If he doesn't sleeps enough, he feels tired.
examples.correct: If he doesn't sleep enough, he feels tired.
examples.note: After doesn't, use the base verb.

examples.wrong: If you mix red and blue, you got purple.
examples.correct: If you mix red and blue, you get purple.
examples.note: A general result needs the present simple.

rules.title: Present simple or continuous
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — Mixing these two is one of the most common mistakes, and it affects every sentence about the present.

**In simple words** — Present simple = routine or fact: `I work in a bank`. Present continuous = now or temporary: `I'm working at home today`.

**The idea** — English has two present tenses. The present simple talks about habits, facts and things that are always true. The present continuous talks about an action in progress now or around now. The choice is about whether the action is a routine or a moment.

**The form**
- present simple: base verb, with `-s` or `-es` after he, she, it
- present simple negative and question: `do` / `does` + base verb
- present continuous: `am` / `is` / `are` + verb + `-ing`
- present continuous negative: `am not` / `isn't` / `aren't` + verb + `-ing`
- present continuous question: `Am` / `Is` / `Are` + subject + verb + `-ing`
- `-ing` spelling: drop silent `e` (make, making); double a final consonant after one short vowel (run, running)
- never mix the two: no `am` plus a base verb, no `do` plus `-ing`

**When it applies**
- Present simple: habits and facts; signal words `always`, `usually`, `every day`, `on Sundays`, `never`
- Present continuous: now and around now; signal words `now`, `at the moment`, `today`, `this week`, `Look!`, `Listen!`
- Temporary situations: present continuous
- Permanent situations: present simple

**When it does NOT apply** — Verbs of state (know, like, want, have for possession) usually stay in the present simple even for now. Test: can you add `every day` or `usually`? Use the present simple. Can you add `now` or `at the moment`? Use the present continuous.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the present simple for an action happening now
- Using the continuous for a routine: the learner thinks all present actions need `-ing`
- Using the continuous for a general fact
- Mixing the forms: `is` plus a base verb, or `do` plus `-ing`

**Register and usage** — Both are neutral. With `always` the continuous can express an annoying habit.

rules.title: Was and were
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You need it to say where you were and how things were in the past.

**In simple words** — `was` with I/he/she/it, `were` with you/we/they: `I was tired`, `They were at home`. Negative: `wasn't`, `weren't`.

**The idea** — `Was` and `were` are the past of `be`. They describe how things were: states, feelings, places, age, jobs and weather in the past. Like `am`, `is`, `are`, they need no other verb before an adjective, a noun or a place.

**The form**
- `I`, `he`, `she`, `it` + `was`; a singular or uncountable noun + `was`
- `you`, `we`, `they` + `were`; a plural noun + `were`
- Negative: `was not` (`wasn't`), `were not` (`weren't`): no `did`
- Question: `Was` / `Were` before the subject: `Was it ...?`, `Were you ...?`
- Question word: `Where were you ...?`, `Why was she ...?`
- Short answers: `Yes, I was` / `No, they weren't`
- Birth: `was born`, `were born`, always with `be`

**When it applies**
- Past states: adjectives (`tired`, `happy`, `late`), places (`at home`), age, jobs, weather
- Signal words: `yesterday`, `last week`, `ago`, `in 2010`, `when I was a child`
- Saying when and where someone was born

**When it does NOT apply** — For the present use `am`, `is`, `are`. With an action verb use the past simple (`went`, `worked`) and `did` in questions and negatives. Test: if an adjective, noun or place follows, use `was` / `were`; if an action verb follows, use the past simple.

**Typical mistakes**
- `was` with `you`, `we`, `they` (`they was`): one form is used for everybody
- `were` with `I`, `he` or a singular noun
- `did` with `be` (`didn't was`, `did you was`), copied from ordinary verbs
- Missing `be` before an adjective or `born` (`I tired`, `I born`)
- `is` / `are` kept with a past time word
- No inversion in questions (`Where you were ...?`)

**Register and usage** — `wasn't` and `weren't` are normal in speech; full forms are used in formal writing.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing** — `You` always takes `were`, even for one person. `If I were` in conditionals is a different rule.
rules.llmDescription: Past of be, was and were, before adjectives, nouns, places and born: they was, I were, didn't was, did you was, missing was (I born), is/are with past time words.

rules.title: There was and there were
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You use it to describe past scenes, memories and stories.

**In simple words** — It is the past of `there is/are`: `There was a cat` (one), `There were two cats` (more than one).

**The idea** — `There was` and `there were` say that something existed or was in a place in the past. They are the past of `there is` and `there are`. The verb agrees with the noun that comes after it, not with `there`.

**The form**
- `there was` + singular noun: `there was a cat`
- `there was` + uncountable noun: `there was some milk`, `there was a lot of traffic`
- `there were` + plural noun: `there were two cars`, `there were many people`
- Negative: `there wasn't a ...`, `there weren't any ...`, or `there was no ...`, `there were no ...`
- Question: `Was there ...?`, `Were there ...?`
- Question word: `How many ... were there?`, `What was there ...?`
- Short answers: `Yes, there was` / `No, there weren't`

**When it applies**
- Describing a place or scene in the past: `in the room`, `at the party`, `in my town`
- Telling a story: signal words `yesterday`, `last night`, `once`, `when I was a child`
- Saying how many or how much there was: `a lot of`, `many`, `no`, numbers

**When it does NOT apply** — For the present use `there is` / `there are`. To describe a thing already mentioned, use `it was` or `they were` + adjective. Test: if you introduce something new, use `there was` / `there were`; if you describe something known, use `it was` / `they were`.

**Typical mistakes**
- `there was` before a plural (`there was many people`): learners use one form for all; the noun after decides
- `there were` before an uncountable noun (`there were a lot of traffic`)
- `it had` or `had` instead of `there was`, copied from languages that say "have" or "it" here
- Missing `there` (`was a lot of noise`)
- `there is` / `there are` kept with a past time word
- Statement order in questions (`there were any ...?`, `how many ... there were?`)

**Register and usage** — In fast casual speech people sometimes say `there was` before a plural, but in writing and careful speech the plural needs `there were`.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing** — In a list, the first noun usually decides: `there was a table and two chairs`.
rules.llmDescription: Past there was and there were: was before plurals, were before uncountables, it had instead of there was, missing there, there is with past time, statement order in questions.

rules.title: Could for past ability
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — It lets you say what you were able to do earlier in life.

**In simple words** — `could` + plain verb: `I could swim when I was five`. Negative: `couldn't`. Same for every person.

**The idea** — `Could` is the past of `can` when we talk about ability: what someone was able to do in general in the past. Like `can`, it is a modal verb: it never changes for the person, and the next verb is in the base form.

**The form**
- Positive: subject + `could` + base verb: no `to`, no `-s`, no past form of the next verb
- Negative: `could not` (`couldn't`) + base verb
- Question: `Could` + subject + base verb: `Could you ...?`
- Short answers: `Yes, I could` / `No, she couldn't`
- No `did`: `could` makes its own questions and negatives
- Same form for all persons: `I could`, `he could`, `they could`

**When it applies**
- General skills in the past: signal words `when I was five`, `as a child`, `at school`, `years ago`
- Something you were not able to do, even once: `couldn't find`, `couldn't sleep`, `couldn't open`
- Senses in the past: `could see`, `could hear`, `could smell`

**When it does NOT apply** — For ability now use `can`. For ONE success in a difficult situation, in a positive sentence, use `was able to` or `managed to`. Test: a general past skill or any negative → `could` / `couldn't`; one positive success on one day → `was able to`.

**Typical mistakes**
- `can` with a past time word (`can swim when I was six`): the present form is kept
- A past form after `could` (`could swam`): the past is already shown in `could`
- `to` after `could` (`could to go`), copied from `was able to`
- `did` with `could` (`didn't could`, `did you could`), copied from ordinary verbs
- Positive `could` for one success (`could pass the exam yesterday`)

**Register and usage** — `couldn't` is normal in speech; `could not` is used in formal writing.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing** — `Could` also makes polite requests (`Could you ...?`) and talks about possibility now; these are other uses. `could have` + past participle is a later rule.
rules.llmDescription: Could and couldn't for past ability: can with past time words, past form or to after could, didn't could, did you could, could for one success, not was able to.

examples.note: Past ability needs could, not can.

examples.correct: She could speak three languages as a child.
examples.note: Use the base form after could.

examples.correct: We couldn't find the hotel last night.

examples.correct: He couldn't sleep because of the noise.

rules.title: When, before and after in the past
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You need it to tell events in order when you tell stories or explain what happened.

**In simple words** — Join two past events with `when`, `before`, `after`; both are in the past simple: `After I finished work, I went home`.

**The idea** — `When`, `before` and `after` join two past events and show their order. Both events are finished, so both parts of the sentence use the past simple. The time word opens one clause; the other clause is the main part and cannot be left out.

**The form**
- `when` + past simple, + past simple: one event right after the other
- `before` + past simple: this clause is the later event
- `after` + past simple: this clause is the earlier event
- Time clause first: put a comma after it; time clause second: no comma
- Negative: `didn't` + base verb in either clause
- Question: question order only in the main clause: `What did you do after ...?`
- The time clause keeps statement order: `after the class finished`, not `after did the class finish`

**When it applies**
- Telling a story or your day: signal words `yesterday`, `last night`, `then`, `first`
- Two short actions, one after another: `when` + `came`, `saw`, `arrived`, `opened`
- Saying which action came first: `before`, `after`

**When it does NOT apply** — For a future event use the present simple after `when`, `before`, `after` (future time clauses). For a long background action use the past continuous with `while` or `when`. Test: both actions finished in the past → past simple in both clauses; the event is still in the future → present simple after the time word.

**Typical mistakes**
- Present simple in the time clause (`after I finish yesterday`): the future pattern is copied into a past story
- Present simple in the main clause (`when she called, I answer`)
- Present perfect with a finished past time (`when they have arrived yesterday`)
- `was` + past form (`when I was opened`), mixing two past patterns
- Question order inside the time clause
- The time clause alone as a full sentence: it needs a main clause

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing** — `before` and `after` can also take `-ing` (`after eating`). With `after`, the past perfect is possible, but the past simple is enough because `after` already shows the order.
rules.llmDescription: Past time clauses with when, before, after: present or present perfect in either clause, was plus past form, question order after the conjunction, time clause standing alone.

examples.wrong: When I get home yesterday, I called my mum.
examples.correct: When I got home yesterday, I called my mum.
examples.note: A past event after when needs the past simple.

examples.correct: After we finished dinner last night, we watched a film.

examples.correct: What did you do after the class finished?

examples.note: Opened needs no was before it.

examples.correct: We went home after the film ended.
examples.note: An after clause cannot stand alone.

rules.title: Present continuous for arrangements
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You use it to arrange meetings, trips and plans with other people.

**In simple words** — Use `am/is/are` + `-ing` for a fixed plan in the near future: `I'm meeting Anna at 6`, `We're flying to Rome on Friday`.

**The idea** — The present continuous can talk about the future when a plan is already fixed: you agreed a time with someone, booked a ticket or made an appointment. The speaker sees the event as already written in the diary, so a present form is used.

**The form**
- `am` / `is` / `are` + verb-`ing` + a future time: `tonight`, `tomorrow`, `on Friday`, `next week`
- Negative: `am not`, `isn't`, `aren't` + verb-`ing`
- Question: `Am` / `Is` / `Are` + subject + verb-`ing`: `What are you doing ...?`, `Are you coming ...?`
- Short forms: `I'm meeting`, `she's flying`, `we're having`
- With `go`: `I'm going to the dentist`, no need for `going to go`
- A future time word, or a clear context, shows it is not now

**When it applies**
- Arrangements with other people: `meeting`, `seeing`, `having dinner with`, `playing ... with`
- Booked travel and events: `flying`, `leaving`, `staying`, `getting married`
- Asking about plans: `What are you doing ...?`, `Are you doing anything ...?`

**When it does NOT apply** — An intention only in your head, or a prediction from what you see, takes `going to`. A decision made now, an offer or a promise takes `will`. Train and film times take the present simple. Test: is it arranged, with a time and other people? → present continuous; just an intention → `going to`; deciding now → `will`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Present simple for a personal arrangement (`I see the dentist at four tomorrow`): learners use one present form for everything
- `do` questions about plans (`What do you do this weekend?`), which ask about habits instead
- Missing `be` (`she flying`) or missing `-ing` (`are have`)
- Using it for things nobody arranges, such as the weather: use `going to` or `will`

**Register and usage** — Very common in everyday speech for weekend and holiday plans; in speech it is more natural than `will` for fixed arrangements.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing** — State verbs (`know`, `like`, `want`) are not used this way.
rules.llmDescription: Present continuous for fixed future arrangements with a time word: present simple or do-question for personal plans, missing be or -ing, weather instead of going to.

rules.title: How much and how many
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You need it to ask about quantity and price, for example when shopping.

**In simple words** — `How many` + countable: `How many people?` `How much` + uncountable: `How much sugar?` `How much` also asks the price: `How much is it?`

**The idea** — `How much` and `how many` ask about quantity. English chooses by the noun: things you can count take `how many`, things you cannot count take `how much`. `How much` also asks about price.

**The form**
- `how many` + plural noun + question order: `how many brothers do you have`
- `how much` + uncountable noun + question order: `how much water do we need`
- Price: `how much is ...?`, `how much are ...?`, `how much does ... cost?`
- The noun comes right after `how many` / `how much`, then the helper and the subject
- With there: `how many ... are there`, `how much ... is there`
- The noun can be dropped when it is clear: `how many do you need`
- When the noun is the subject, no `do`: `how many people came`

**When it applies**
- Counting people and things: `people`, `books`, `times`, `days`, `children`
- Amounts of uncountable things: `money`, `time`, `water`, `sugar`, `homework`
- Prices in shops and cafes

**When it does NOT apply** — In statements and negatives use `many`, `much` or `a lot of` (the much/many rule). For age use `how old`, for distance `how far`. Test: is it a question that starts with `how` and asks about amount? → this rule; is it a statement about amount? → the much/many rule.

**Typical mistakes**
- `how much` + plural (`how much books`): learners choose by size, not by countability
- `how many` + uncountable (`how many money`, `how many sugar`)
- A singular noun after `how many` (`how many day`)
- The noun moved away from `how many` (`how many do you have brothers`)
- Missing `do` / `does` or wrong order (`how much time she spends`)
- `how much costs it` instead of `how much does it cost`

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing** — `people` is plural, so `how many people`; `money`, `advice`, `news`, `information` are uncountable, so `how much`.
rules.llmDescription: Questions with how much, how many: how much with plurals, how many with uncountables, singular noun after how many, noun separated, missing do, how much costs it.

rules.title: Subject and object questions
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — It stops a very common mistake with helper verbs when you ask "who" or "what".

**In simple words** — If `who`/`what` is the doer, use no `do/did`: `Who called you?` If it is the receiver, use `did`: `Who did you call?`

**The idea** — When `who` or `what` asks about the doer of the action (the subject), the question keeps statement order and needs no `do`, `does` or `did`. When it asks about the person or thing that receives the action (the object), the normal question pattern with a helper is used.

**The form**
- Subject question: `who` / `what` / `which` + noun + main verb: `who lives`, `what happened`
- Present subject question: the verb takes `-s`: `who knows`, `what makes`
- Past subject question: past form: `who called`, `what broke`
- `how many` + noun as the subject: `how many people came`
- Object question: wh-word + `do` / `does` / `did` + subject + base verb: `who did you see`
- With `be` and modals nothing changes: `who is`, `who can`
- Negative subject question: `who didn't come`: `did` appears only with `not`

**When it applies**
- Asking who did something: `who` + `called`, `won`, `took`, `made`, `broke`
- Asking what caused something: `what happened`, `what made`
- Signal: the answer word is the subject of the answer sentence

**When it does NOT apply** — When the wh-word is the object, use `do` / `does` / `did` as in ordinary questions. Test: answer with a full sentence; if the answer word stands before the verb, it is a subject question, no helper; if it stands after the verb, add the helper.

**Typical mistakes**
- `did` or `does` in a subject question (`who did call`, `what did happen`): every question seems to need a helper
- No `-s` in a present subject question (`who live here`)
- Base verb instead of the past form (`who break` about yesterday)
- No helper in an object question (`who you met`), overusing the subject pattern

**Register and usage** — `whom` for objects is formal and rare; `who` is normal in speech and writing.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing** — `who` takes a singular verb by default: `who wants`. A stressed `did` (`who DID call?`) is emphatic and rare.
rules.llmDescription: Wh-questions where who, what, which or how many is the subject (no do/does/did) versus the object (helper needed): who did call, what did happen, who live, who you met.

rules.title: Too, also and either
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You use it every time you agree or add something: "me too", "I don't either".

**In simple words** — Positive: `I like it too` or `I also like it`. Negative: `I don't like it either`.

**The idea** — `Too`, `also` and `either` add a second, similar fact. `Too` and `also` add to positive sentences; `either` adds to negative ones. They also stand in different places in the sentence.

**The form**
- `too` at the end of a positive clause: `..., too`
- `also` in the middle: before the main verb (`also likes`), after `be` (`is also`), after the first helper or modal (`can also`, `have also`)
- `either` at the end of a negative clause: `don't ... either`, `isn't ... either`
- Short replies: `Me too` after a positive; `Me neither` after a negative
- Positive questions take `too`: `Are you coming too?`
- `too` and `also` are not used in negative clauses with this meaning

**When it applies**
- Adding another fact about the same person or thing: `also`, `too`
- Saying another person is the same: `too` (positive), `either` (negative)
- Signal words: `and`, a second clause, `not`, `never`

**When it does NOT apply** — `too` before an adjective means "more than OK" (`too hot`): that is the enough/too rule. Answers like `So do I` and `Neither do I` are a separate pattern. Test: is the clause negative? → `either` at the end; positive → `too` at the end or `also` in the middle.

**Typical mistakes**
- `too` in a negative clause (`doesn't eat it too`): one word is used for all sentences
- `also` in a negative clause instead of `either`
- `either` in a positive clause
- `also` after the main verb (`plays also`, `have also a cat`), copied from other languages
- `Me too` after a negative sentence instead of `Me neither`

**Register and usage** — `too` is more common in speech, `also` in writing. `Me either` is informal American; `Me neither` is standard.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing** — `as well` means the same as `too` and also goes at the end.
rules.llmDescription: Additive too, also, either: too or also in negative clauses, either in positive clauses, also after the main verb, me too after a negative; not too plus adjective.

rules.title: Somebody, anything, nobody, everyone
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You use these words all the time to talk about people, things and places without naming them.

**In simple words** — `something`, `anyone`, `nobody`, `everywhere` are treated as singular: `Everyone is here`. Use `some-` in positive sentences, `any-` in negatives and questions.

**The idea** — Words made from `some-`, `any-`, `no-`, `every-` + `-body`, `-one`, `-thing`, `-where` talk about people, things and places without naming them. They are singular words, and words that describe them come after them, not before.

**The form**
- People: `somebody` / `someone`, `anybody` / `anyone`, `nobody` / `no one`, `everybody` / `everyone`
- Things: `something`, `anything`, `nothing`, `everything`
- Places: `somewhere`, `anywhere`, `nowhere`, `everywhere`
- Singular verb: `everybody is`, `nobody knows`, `something has`
- Adjective after: `something nice`, `nothing new`, `somewhere quiet`
- `else` after: `someone else`, `anything else`
- `they` / `their` can refer back: `everyone ... their`
- One word, except `no one` (also `no-one`)

**When it applies**
- An unknown person, thing or place: `some-`, `any-`
- All people or things: `every-`
- Zero: `no-` with a positive verb
- Describing the word: an adjective or `else` follows it

**When it does NOT apply** — Choosing between `some-` and `any-` (statement vs negative or question) is the some/any rule; `no-` words together with `not` is the one-negative rule. Test: is the problem the verb form, the place of the adjective or `else`, or the word itself? → this rule; is it `some-` vs `any-`? → the some/any rule.

**Typical mistakes**
- Plural verb after `every-` (`everybody are`): the meaning is many people, but the form is singular
- Adjective before the word (`nice something`), copied from normal noun order
- `else` before the word (`else anyone`)
- `every people` instead of `everyone`; `somebody of` instead of `one of`

**Register and usage** — `-one` and `-body` mean the same; `-one` is slightly more common in writing.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing** — `everyone` (all people) is different from `every one` (each single item, two words).
rules.llmDescription: Compounds somebody, anyone, nothing, everything, somewhere: plural verb after everybody or nobody, adjective or else placed before (nice something, else anyone), every people, somebody of. Not some/any choice.

rules.title: One negative per clause
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — In many languages two negatives are normal; in English they sound wrong, so this mistake is easy to make.

**In simple words** — Use only one negative word: `I don't know anything` or `I know nothing`, not "I don't know nothing".

**The idea** — Standard English uses only ONE negative word in a clause. Words like `never`, `nobody`, `nothing`, `nowhere`, `no` and `none` are already negative, so the verb stays positive. A second negative can cancel the first or make the speech sound wrong.

**The form**
- `not` / `n't` + `any-` word: `don't know anything`, `didn't see anybody`, `won't go anywhere`
- Positive verb + `no-` word: `know nothing`, `saw nobody`, `went nowhere`
- `never` + positive verb: `never eats`, `has never been`
- `no` + noun with a positive verb: `there is no ...`; or `not any`: `there isn't any ...`
- Negative subject + positive verb: `nobody came`, `nothing happened`, `none of us knew`
- `hardly` is negative too: `can hardly`, not `can't hardly`
- The same in every tense, with modals and in imperatives

**When it applies**
- Any clause with `not`, `never`, `no`, `nobody`, `no one`, `nothing`, `nowhere`, `none`, `hardly`
- Answers, stories, warnings and orders that say "zero"

**When it does NOT apply** — Building the basic negative with `do not` / `does not` is the present simple negation rule; choosing `some` or `any` is the some/any rule. Test: count the negative words in the clause; if there are two, keep one: `not` + `any-` word, or a `no-` word with a positive verb.

**Typical mistakes**
- `not` + `no-` word (`don't know nothing`), copied from languages where two negatives are normal
- `never` + `not` (`never doesn't`, `hasn't never`)
- Negative subject + negative verb (`nobody didn't`)
- `not` + `hardly` (`can't hardly`)

**Register and usage** — Double negatives appear in songs, films and some dialects, but in standard speech and in writing they are mistakes. Learners hear them in music and copy them.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing** — `not` + a negative adjective (`not unusual`, `not impossible`) is correct, careful style: it means "quite usual" or "possible".

rules.title: Prepositions of movement
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You need them for directions, travel and telling a story about where people went.

**In simple words** — They show the way: `to` the station, `into` the room, `out of` the car, `across` the road, `through` the park, `up` and `down` the stairs.

**The idea** — Prepositions of movement show where someone or something goes: the goal or the path. They follow movement verbs like `go`, `walk`, `run`, `drive`, `fall`, `get`. Each one draws a different picture of the way.

**The form**
- `to` — the goal: `go to school`, `walk to the park`
- `into` / `out of` — entering or leaving a space: `into the room`, `out of the car`
- `onto` / `off` — onto a surface or away from it: `onto the table`, `off the bike`
- `across` — from one side to the other of a flat thing: `across the road`, `across the bridge`
- `through` — inside something, from one end to the other: `through the tunnel`, `through the forest`
- `along`, `past`, `up`, `down`, `towards`, `over`, `around` — the line or direction of the way
- No `to` before `home`, `here`, `there`: `go home`
- `arrive in` + city or country, `arrive at` + building or station, never `arrive to`
- Transport: `get on` / `get off` a bus, train, plane; `get in` / `get out of` a car or taxi

**When it applies**
- A verb of movement + where to or which way: `go`, `come`, `walk`, `run`, `drive`, `jump`, `fall`
- Directions on the street and travel

**When it does NOT apply** — For position, where something simply is, use `in`, `on`, `at` (prepositions of place). Test: does the verb show movement to a new place or along a way? → `to`, `into`, `across`, `through`; is the thing just there? → `in`, `on`, `at`.

**Typical mistakes**
- `to` before `home` (`go to home`): learners add `to` after every `go`
- `arrive to`, copied from `go to`
- `at` or `in` for the goal after `go` (`go at the supermarket`)
- `across` and `through` mixed up: flat surface vs inside
- `of` instead of `off` (`fell of`); `out` without `of` (`got out the taxi`)
- `get in` with buses and trains; `towards to`

**Register and usage** — In relaxed speech `in` and `on` often replace `into` and `onto` after `jump` or `put`; this is accepted.
rules.llmDescription: Movement prepositions to, into, out of, off, across, through, towards after go, arrive, get: go to home, arrive to, go at, across vs through, fell of, get in the bus.

rules.title: Present perfect with for and since
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You use it to say how long something has lasted: your job, where you live, how long you know someone.

**In simple words** — `have/has` + past participle: `I have lived here for five years` (a period) or `since 2020` (a starting point). It is still true now.

**The idea** — When a situation began in the past and is still true now, English connects both times in one verb form, the present perfect. The speaker says: it started then and it continues until now. The words `for` and `since` measure this period.

**The form**
- `have/has` + past participle: `have lived`, `has worked`, `has been`
- Negative: `have not` (`haven't`) / `has not` (`hasn't`) + participle
- Question: `Have/Has` + subject + participle; `How long have you ...?`
- `for` + length of time: `for two years`, `for a long time`, `for ages`
- `since` + starting point: `since 2010`, `since Monday`, `since I was a child`
- Regular participles end in `-ed`; irregular ones must be learned: `known`, `been`, `had`

**When it applies**
- A state or action that began earlier and continues now: signal words `for`, `since`, `how long`
- With state verbs: `be`, `know`, `have`, `live`, `work`
- With `all day`, `all my life`, `recently` for unfinished periods

**When it does NOT apply** — If the situation is finished or the time is named as past (`in 2010`, `last year`), use the past simple. Test: if it still goes on now, use the present perfect with `for/since`; if it is over, use the past simple.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the present simple (`live ... since 2018`), because the situation is true now; English needs the perfect
- Mixing up `for` and `since` (`since five years`, `for 2010`); `for` takes a length, `since` takes a starting point
- Using the past simple in `how long` questions about the present
- Using the base form or the past form instead of the participle

**Register and usage** — Contractions (`I've`, `she's`) are normal in speech and informal writing.

rules.title: Present perfect with ever and never
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You need it to talk about life experience in interviews, small talk and travel stories.

**In simple words** — `Have you ever been to Paris?` `I have never tried sushi.` No exact time is given; it is about experience in your life up to now.

**The idea** — To talk about life experience without saying when it happened, English uses the present perfect. The exact time is not important; what matters is whether the experience exists in a person's life up to now.

**The form**
- `have/has` + past participle: `have been`, `has seen`, `have eaten`
- `ever` in questions: `Have you ever ...?` and after superlatives: `the best film I have ever seen`
- `never` in statements: `have never` + participle; it already means `not ever`
- Negative with `not`: `haven't` + participle (without `never`); never use `not` and `never` together
- Position: `ever` and `never` go between `have/has` and the participle
- `been` for visits that are finished (`have been to Rome`); `gone` means the person is still there

**When it applies**
- Asking about experience: signal words `ever`, `before`, `so far`, `in your life`
- Denying experience: `never`, `not yet`
- Superlatives of experience: `the most ... I have ever`

**When it does NOT apply** — With a specific past time (`last year`, `in 2015`, `yesterday`) use the past simple. Test: if you can add a finished time, use the past simple; if the time is open, use the present perfect.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `ever` in positive statements (`I have ever been`), because `ever` seems to mean 'once'; use `never` or no adverb
- Using the past form or base form instead of the participle (`ever ate`, `ever play`)
- Double negatives: `haven't never`, `has never not`
- Putting `never` in front of `have`

**Register and usage** — `ever` is the natural word in questions and superlatives; `never` is common in speech.
rules.llmDescription: Present perfect for life experience with ever and never: ever in positive statements, never with not, never before have, wrong participle, been or gone, present perfect with a past time.

rules.title: Past simple or present perfect
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — Choosing between these two tenses is one of the most frequent problems at this level.

**In simple words** — A finished time (`yesterday`, `in 2019`) = past simple: `I saw it yesterday`. A link with now, or no time given = present perfect: `I have lost my keys`.

**The idea** — Both tenses talk about the past, but they look from different places. The past simple closes the event in a finished time. The present perfect keeps a link with now: the time is not finished, or the result matters today.

**The form**
- Past simple: verb + `-ed`, or the irregular past form — `finished`, `went`
- Present perfect: `have` / `has` + past participle — `has finished`, `have gone`
- Negative: `didn't` + base verb / `haven't` + participle
- Question: `Did` + subject + base verb / `Have` + subject + participle
- Past simple goes with a finished time: `yesterday`, `last week`, `in 2019`, `ago`, `when`
- Present perfect goes with an open time: `already`, `yet`, `just`, `ever`, `never`, `so far`, `today`, `this week`
- The question `When ...?` takes the past simple

**When it applies**
- Past simple: a named or known finished time, a story told in order, a person who is no longer alive
- Present perfect: experience up to now, a recent action with a result now, news, a period that is still open

**When it does NOT apply** — Never use the present perfect with a finished-time word. Test: can you add `yesterday`, `last year` or `ago`? Use the past simple. Can you add `so far`, `already` or `yet`? Use the present perfect.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the present perfect with `yesterday`, `ago` or `last`: learners link any past event to the present
- Asking `When have you ...?`: the question about time needs the past simple
- Using the past simple for a period still open (`so far today`)
- Using the present perfect for a person who has died
- Mixing the two inside one story

**Register and usage** — Spoken American English often uses the past simple with `already` and `just`; formal and British English prefers the present perfect there.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `Been` with a past time word (`last summer`) is a past simple context: use `went` or `was`
- `This morning` is past simple after midday, present perfect before it
rules.llmDescription: Choice between past simple and present perfect: present perfect with yesterday, ago, last, in 2019 or when; past simple for an open period or result now.

rules.title: The first conditional
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You use it for real plans, warnings and promises about the future.

**In simple words** — `If` + present, `will` + verb: `If it rains, we will stay home`. It speaks about a real possibility.

**The idea** — The first conditional speaks about a real, possible situation in the future and its likely result. The speaker thinks the condition may well happen, so the sentence has two parts: the `if` part and the result part.

**The form**
- `if` + present simple, `will` + base verb: the condition is in the present form, the result in the future form
- The result clause can come first, without a comma: result + `if` + present simple
- Negative: `if you don't ...`, `will not` / `won't`; `unless` + positive verb means `if not`
- Question: `What will you do if ...?`; the `if` part stays in the present simple
- Other results: `can`, `may`, `might` or an imperative instead of `will`
- Never put `will` right after `if` (`if it will rain`)

**When it applies**
- Real future possibilities: signal words `if`, `unless`, `as soon as`, `when`
- Warnings, promises and threats
- Plans that depend on something else, such as weather or time

**When it does NOT apply** — For an unlikely or imaginary situation use the second conditional (`if` + past); for a general truth use the present simple in both parts. Test: if the condition is realistic and about the future, use present + `will`; if it is imaginary, use past + `would`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `will` in the `if` clause, because the meaning is future; English uses the present simple there
- Using `would` or the present simple in the result, so the result loses its future meaning
- Using `unless` with a negative verb (a double negative)

**Register and usage** — Both orders are normal; put a comma after the `if` clause when it comes first.
rules.llmDescription: First conditional if plus present simple with will in the result: will after if, would in the result, unless with a negative verb, wrong tense for a real future possibility.

examples.correct: If it rains, we will stay at home.
examples.note: Use the present simple after 'if', 'will' in the result.

examples.wrong: If you will come, I will cook dinner.
examples.correct: If you come, I will cook dinner.

examples.wrong: I call you if I will have time.
examples.correct: I will call you if I have time.

examples.wrong: If she studies hard, she would pass the exam.

rules.title: Must and have to
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You need it to talk about rules and obligations at work, school and when you travel.

**In simple words** — `must` = a strong need that comes from you or a strong rule. `have to` = a rule from outside: `I have to wear a uniform`.

**The idea** — English has two ways to say that something is necessary. `Must` usually shows the speaker's own feeling or a strong rule, while `have to` shows an outside rule or a fact. Their negatives mean very different things.

**The form**
- `must` + base verb: one form for all persons; no `to`, no `-s`
- `have to` + base verb: `have to` with `I/you/we/they`, `has to` with `he/she/it`
- Negative of `have to`: `don't/doesn't have to` + base verb: not necessary
- Negative of `must`: `must not` / `mustn't` + base verb: forbidden
- Questions: `Do you have to ...?` for `have to`; `Must I ...?` is formal and rare
- Past: `must` has no past form, so use `had to` + base verb; questions and negatives use `did` + `have to`

**When it applies**
- Rules, laws and instructions: signal words `must not`, `you have to`, `it is necessary`
- Duties from work, school or other people
- The speaker's strong personal need: `must call`

**When it does NOT apply** — For advice use `should`; for permission and ability use `can`. Test: if the meaning is 'it is not necessary', use `don't have to`; if it is 'it is forbidden', use `mustn't`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `mustn't` for 'not necessary', because the negative of `have to` is not learned
- Adding `to` after `must` (`must to go`), or using `do` with `must`
- Writing `haves to` or `have to` after `he/she`
- Using `must` for the past

**Register and usage** — `have to` is the common spoken form; `must` is typical for signs, rules and formal instructions.

rules.title: Verb plus -ing form
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — Many everyday verbs (enjoy, finish, avoid) need this pattern, and the wrong one is a common mistake.

**In simple words** — After some verbs use verb + `-ing`: `I enjoy reading`, `She finished working`. Not "enjoy to read". It is also used after prepositions: `interested in learning`.

**The idea** — Some English verbs are followed by another verb in the `-ing` form (the gerund), and not by `to` + verb. The first verb decides the pattern, so these combinations are learned in groups. The same form is used after prepositions.

**The form**
- Verb + `-ing`: `enjoy doing`, `finish working`, `avoid driving`
- Verbs of liking and dislike: `enjoy`, `mind`, `can't stand`, `don't mind`
- Verbs of ending and continuing: `finish`, `stop`, `keep`, `give up`, `carry on`
- Verbs of avoiding and suggesting: `avoid`, `suggest`, `practise`, `consider`, `imagine`
- After every preposition: `interested in learning`, `thinking about changing`, `look forward to seeing`
- The negative puts `not` before the `-ing` form: `not going`; the `-ing` form can also be the subject: `swimming is fun`

**When it applies**
- After the verbs above: signal words `enjoy`, `finish`, `avoid`, `suggest`, `mind`
- After a preposition, including `to` in `look forward to` and `be used to`
- As a noun-like subject: `reading helps`

**When it does NOT apply** — After verbs such as `want`, `decide`, `hope`, `need`, `plan`, `learn` use `to` + base verb; after modals use the bare verb. Test: if the first verb is on the `enjoy/finish/avoid/suggest` list or the word before is a preposition, use `-ing`; if it is `want/decide/hope`, use `to`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `to` + verb after the `-ing` group (`enjoy to cook`), because many verbs take `to`
- Using the base form after a preposition (`interested in learn`)
- Treating `to` in `look forward to` as an infinitive marker
- Confusing `stop doing` (end an action) with `stop to do` (pause in order to do)

**Register and usage** — This pattern is neutral and frequent in all registers.
rules.llmDescription: Verbs and prepositions followed by the -ing form: enjoy, finish, avoid, suggest, keep, mind, stop, look forward to; to-infinitive or base verb used where -ing is required.

rules.title: Verb plus to-infinitive
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You use it to talk about wishes, plans and decisions.

**In simple words** — After verbs like `want`, `hope`, `decide`, `plan` use `to` + plain verb: `I want to go`. Learn each verb with its pattern.

**The idea** — Some verbs name a wish, a plan or a decision, and the thing wished or planned comes in a second verb. After many of these verbs English uses `to` + base verb. The first verb decides the pattern, so each verb must be learned with its pattern.

**The form**
- `verb` + `to` + base verb — `want to go`, `decide to buy`
- With an object: `verb` + person + `to` + base verb — `want you to come`, `ask him to help`
- Negative: put `not` before `to` — `decided not to go`; or negate the first verb
- Question: auxiliary + subject + first verb + `to` + base verb
- The first verb changes for person and tense; `to` + verb never changes
- Common verbs: `want`, `would like`, `hope`, `plan`, `decide`, `promise`, `refuse`, `agree`, `manage`, `learn`, `need`, `afford`, `seem`
- Verbs with a person: `ask`, `tell`, `want`, `teach`, `allow`, `expect`

**When it applies**
- Wishes and hopes: `want`, `hope`, `would like`
- Plans and decisions: `plan`, `decide`, `choose`
- Promises, agreements and refusals
- Ability and success: `learn`, `manage`

**When it does NOT apply** — After modal verbs (`can`, `must`, `will`) use the bare verb with no `to`. After verbs such as `enjoy`, `avoid`, `finish` use the `-ing` form. Test: if the verb is a modal, use no `to`; if it names a plan or wish, use `to`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Leaving out `to` (`want go`): learners copy the bare verb pattern of modals
- Using `-ing` instead of `to` (`decided buying`): they mix the two patterns
- Using `that` clauses instead of an object + `to` (`want that you come`)
- Adding `to` after a modal or after `let` and `make`

**Register and usage** — Neutral; `would like to` is polite, `want to` is direct.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- A few verbs take both patterns with the same meaning (`start`, `begin`, `like`)
- Some verbs change meaning with `to` or `-ing`, which is a separate rule

rules.title: The past continuous
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — It makes your stories richer: you can set the scene and say what was going on when something happened.

**In simple words** — `was/were` + `-ing`: `I was cooking when you called`. A long background action is interrupted by a short one.

**The idea** — The past continuous shows an action that was in progress at a moment in the past. It sets the scene, and it often describes a long action that another, shorter action interrupted.

**The form**
- Positive: `was/were` + verb + `-ing`: `I was working`, `they were working`
- `was` with `I`, `he`, `she`, `it`; `were` with `you`, `we`, `they`
- Negative: `was not` (`wasn't`), `were not` (`weren't`) + `-ing`
- Question: `Was/Were` + subject + `-ing`: `what were you doing`
- No `did` in this tense; the `-ing` spelling follows the same rules as the present continuous
- Linking words: `while`, `when`, `as` + the past continuous or the past simple

**When it applies**
- An action in progress at a stated time: signal words `at 8 o'clock`, `all evening`, `at that moment`
- A long action interrupted by a short one: `was walking when it started`
- Two actions going on at the same time: `while`
- Background description in stories

**When it does NOT apply** — For a completed action or one event after another, use the past simple. Test: if the action was already going on when something else happened, use the continuous for the long action and the simple for the short one.

**Typical mistakes**
- Leaving out the `-ing` form (`was watch`), or leaving out `was/were`
- Mixing `was` and `were` (`they was`, `he were`)
- Using the past simple for a background action in progress
- Using `did` with the past continuous (`didn't be waiting`)

**Register and usage** — It is common in storytelling, in spoken and written narrative.

rules.title: Used to for past habits
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — It lets you say how life was before and is not now.

**In simple words** — `I used to live in Kyiv` = I lived there before, not now. Negative and question: `didn't use to`, `Did you use to...?`

**The idea** — `Used to` talks about habits and states that were true in the past but are not true now. It stresses the contrast with the present. English has a special form because the past simple alone does not show that the situation has ended.

**The form**
- Positive: `used to` + base verb — `used to live`, `used to play`
- Negative: `didn't use to` + base verb (no `-d` on `use`)
- Question: `Did` + subject + `use to` + base verb
- Short answers: `Yes, I did` / `No, I didn't`
- The form is the same for all persons; there is no present form
- With the past simple, the `-d` is only on `used`, in positive sentences
- Time phrases are general: `as a child`, `when I was young`, `years ago`

**When it applies**
- Past habits that stopped: `used to go`, `used to play`
- Past states that changed: `used to be`, `used to have`, `used to like`
- Contrast with now: signal words `now`, `any more`, `but now`

**When it does NOT apply** — For a single event or an exact time, use the past simple. For a repeated action with no contrast, `would` is also possible, but only for actions, not states. `Be used to` + `-ing` means "be accustomed to", not a past habit. Test: if it happened once, or at a named time, use the past simple; if it was regular and is over, use `used to`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Writing `use to` in a positive sentence, because `didn't use to` has no `-d`; the positive keeps `-d`
- Writing `didn't used to`, because the past is shown already by `did`
- Adding `-ing` or `-s` after `used to`: the verb that follows is always the bare verb
- Using `used to` with a single event or an exact date
- Mixing it up with `be used to`: `was used to play`

**Register and usage** — Neutral and very common in speech and writing; in formal writing `did not use to` and `used not to` both appear.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `Would` replaces `used to` for repeated actions, never for states
- There is no `used to` for the present; use `usually` or the present simple

rules.title: Defining relative clauses
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — It lets you say exactly which person or thing you mean and build longer, natural sentences.

**In simple words** — Use `who`, `which` or `that` to say which one: `The man who lives next door is a doctor`. `who` for people, `which` for things, `that` for both.

**The idea** — A defining relative clause tells the listener which person or thing you mean. Without it the noun would be unclear. The clause comes right after the noun and starts with a relative pronoun.

**The form**
- People: `who` or `that`: `the woman who works here`
- Things and animals: `which` or `that`: `the book which I read`
- Possession: `whose` + noun: `the man whose car was stolen`
- Places: `where`; times: `when`; reasons: `why`
- No commas around the clause
- The pronoun replaces the noun, so do not repeat it: no `she`, `it`, `them` after it
- The pronoun can be left out when it is the object: `the book I read`, `the man you met`; never when it is the subject
- The verb agrees with the noun before the pronoun

**When it applies**
- Identifying a noun: signal words `the one who`, `the thing that`, `a person who`
- Definitions: `a mechanic is a person who ...`
- Choosing between similar things

**When it does NOT apply** — If the clause only adds extra information and is set off by commas, use a non-defining clause, where `that` is not possible. Test: if you can delete the clause and the noun is still clear, it is non-defining; if you cannot, it is defining.

**Typical mistakes**
- Repeating the noun with a pronoun (`the car that I bought it`), because the sentence is built like a main clause
- Using `which` for people and `who` for things
- Using `what` as a relative pronoun (`the book what`)
- Adding commas that make the clause non-defining
- Singular verb after a plural antecedent

**Register and usage** — `that` is neutral; `who` and `which` are slightly more formal.

rules.title: The simple passive
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You meet it in news, signs, instructions and formal texts, and use it when the doer is unknown or not important.

**In simple words** — `be` + past participle: `The window was broken`, `English is spoken here`. The focus is on what happened, not on who did it.

**The idea** — In the passive the subject of the sentence is the person or thing that receives the action. English uses it when the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious, or when you want to begin with the thing affected.

**The form**
- Present passive: `am/is/are` + past participle: `is made`, `are sold`
- Past passive: `was/were` + past participle: `was built`, `were taken`
- Negative: `is not`, `was not` + participle; question: `Is it made ...?`, `where were they taken`
- The doer, if mentioned, comes after `by`: `by the police`
- The participle is the third form of the verb: regular `-ed`, irregular `stolen`, `written`
- `be` agrees with the new subject, not with the doer

**When it applies**
- The doer is unknown or unimportant: signal words `was stolen`, `is made`, `are spoken`
- Processes, facts and news: `is produced in`, `was founded in`
- Formal and written texts, signs, instructions

**When it does NOT apply** — If the doer is the important subject, use the active form; intransitive verbs (`arrive`, `happen`) have no passive. Test: if the sentence needs an object that becomes the subject, the passive is possible; if there is no object, it is not.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the base form or the active form after `be` (`was break`), instead of the participle
- Using the wrong `be` (`letters was sent`) because the doer or the last noun is used for agreement
- Using `did` for a negative passive (`didn't made`)
- Mixing up `by` with other prepositions

**Register and usage** — The passive is common in news, science and formal writing and less so in casual speech.

rules.title: Question tags
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — It makes your conversation sound natural when you check information or look for agreement.

**In simple words** — A short question at the end: `You're tired, aren't you?` A positive sentence takes a negative tag, a negative sentence a positive tag: `She can swim, can't she?`

**The idea** — A question tag is a short question added to a statement. The speaker uses it to check information or to ask the listener to agree. English builds the tag from the helper verb of the statement, turned around, with the opposite polarity.

**The form**
- Positive statement + negative tag: `are tired`, `aren't you`
- Negative statement + positive tag: `aren't tired`, `are you`
- The tag uses the same auxiliary as the statement: `is`, `has`, `can`, `will`, `would`
- With no auxiliary (present simple), use `do` / `does`; for the past simple use `did`
- The tag has a pronoun subject, never a noun: `it`, `he`, `they`
- Special tags: `I am` → `aren't I`; `let's` → `shall we`; imperatives → `will you` / `won't you`
- Words with a negative meaning (`never`, `hardly`, `nobody`, `nothing`) count as negative: positive tag
- `Everyone`, `nobody`, `someone` take `they`; `nothing`, `something` take `it`

**When it applies**
- Checking facts you are nearly sure of (falling intonation)
- Asking for agreement or confirmation (rising or falling tone)
- Making polite requests and invitations

**When it does NOT apply** — For a real question without an expected answer, use a normal question or a yes/no question. Test: if you expect "yes", use a tag; if you do not know, ask directly.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the same polarity (`are tired, are you`): this only appears in special tones
- Repeating the main verb instead of the auxiliary
- Forgetting `do` / `does` / `did` for the simple tenses
- Using a noun, or the wrong pronoun, in the tag

**Register and usage** — Very common in spoken English, much less in formal writing. Intonation changes the meaning from a real question to a request for agreement.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `Let's` takes `shall we`; imperatives take `will you` or `won't you`
- American speakers also use `right?` and `OK?` as tags

examples.correct: She has finished the book, hasn't she?
examples.note: The tag repeats the auxiliary has.
