examples.correct: Nobody called yesterday, did they?
examples.note: Nobody is negative, so the tag is positive.

rules.title: Reported statements and backshift
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You need it to retell what someone said, at work, in daily life and in news.

**In simple words** — Usually the verb steps back one tense: "I am tired" → `She said she was tired`. Pronouns and time words change too.

**The idea** — When you report what someone said, you tell it from a later point in time. Because of this shift, the verb usually moves one step back into the past, and pronouns and time words change to fit the new speaker.

**The form**
- Reporting verb + (`that`) + clause: `she said that ...`, `he told me that ...`
- `say` has no object; `tell` needs a person: `said`, but `told me`, `told him`
- Backshift: present simple becomes past simple; present continuous becomes past continuous; present perfect and past simple become past perfect
- Modals: `will` becomes `would`, `can` becomes `could`, `may` becomes `might`; `must` often becomes `had to`
- Pronouns follow the new speaker; time words shift: `today` becomes `that day`, `tomorrow` becomes `the next day`, `now` becomes `then`
- Word order stays that of a statement; there are no quotation marks

**When it applies**
- Reporting past speech or thought: signal words `said`, `told`, `explained`, `mentioned`
- News, messages and retelling of conversations

**When it does NOT apply** — If the reporting is in the present (`she says`) or the fact is still true and just said, the tense can stay unchanged. Test: if the reporting verb is past, move the tense back; if it is present, keep it.

**Typical mistakes**
- Keeping the original present tense after `said`, because the fact feels current
- Using `said me` or `told that` without the person; `tell` needs an object and `say` does not
- Forgetting to change pronouns and time words
- Changing the tense only in one verb of a long report

**Register and usage** — In casual speech people often keep the original tense for fresh news; careful writing shifts it.
rules.llmDescription: Reported statements with said and told: say/tell confusion, missing backshift of present to past and will to would, unchanged pronouns or time words, missing object after tell.

examples.note: The reported clause needs the past form.

examples.correct: They said that they would come.

examples.note: Move the negative back to the past.

rules.title: Present tense in future time clauses
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — "When I will come" is a very common error, and this rule fixes it in every plan and promise.

**In simple words** — After `when`, `before`, `as soon as`, `until`, `if` use the present for the future: `I'll call you when I arrive` (not "will arrive").

**The idea** — When we talk about the future after a time word such as `when` or `as soon as`, English does not repeat `will`. The main clause already says that the action is in the future, so the time clause uses a present form. The same is true for `if`.

**The form**
- main clause: `will` + base verb (or `going to`, or an imperative)
- time clause: conjunction + subject + present simple
- the time clause can come first, with a comma, or second, without one
- present simple has `-s` after he, she, it
- negative time clause: `do not` / `does not` + base verb
- present perfect is possible after `when`, `after`, `until`, `as soon as`: `have` / `has` + past participle
- never `will` or `going to` right after the conjunction

**When it applies**
- Conjunctions of time: `when`, `as soon as`, `before`, `after`, `until`, `while`, `once`, `by the time`
- The condition conjunction `if` and `unless`
- Promises, plans and predictions about the future

**When it does NOT apply** — A question word clause that asks for information keeps `will`, such as `I don't know when she will come`. Test: is the clause a time condition for another action (use the present), or is it the object of a verb like know or ask (the future form stays)?

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `will` in the time clause: the learner copies the main clause form
- Using `going to` after the conjunction
- Dropping the third person `-s`
- Using `will` with `if` as well
- Choosing the present perfect when two actions happen at the same time

**Register and usage** — Neutral in all registers. In writing, the present perfect after `once` and `after` shows that the first action is finished.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `when` as a question word keeps `will`
- `if` meaning `whether` keeps `will` too
rules.llmDescription: Future time clauses: when, as soon as, before, after, until, once, if + present simple, will in the main clause; error is will or going to after the conjunction.

rules.title: Mustn't or don't have to
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — Mixing them up means saying the opposite of what you mean, for example about rules and signs.

**In simple words** — `You mustn't smoke here` = it is forbidden. `You don't have to come` = it is not necessary, but you may.

**The idea** — In the positive, `must` and `have to` are close. In the negative they split completely. `mustn't` says that something is forbidden; `don't have to` says that something is not necessary but still allowed. Mixing them reverses the meaning.

**The form**
- `mustn't` (or `must not`) + base verb: prohibition
- `don't have to` / `doesn't have to` + base verb: no obligation
- `must` has one form for every person; it has no `-s`, no past form of its own
- `have to` is an ordinary verb: `has to` after he, she, it
- question with `have to`: `Do` / `Does` + subject + `have to` + base verb
- question with `must` is rare and formal; use `have to` in speech
- past of `don't have to`: `didn't have to` + base verb
- no `do` or `does` is used with `must`

**When it applies**
- Prohibition: laws, signs, school and workplace rules, safety; signal words: `forbidden`, `not allowed`, `dangerous`
- No necessity: options, free things, things that other people already did; signal words: `free`, `optional`, `no need`

**When it does NOT apply** — `needn't` and `don't need to` also mean no obligation. `can't` can be used for a rule from another person, such as a sign. Test: does the speaker want to stop the action (use `mustn't`) or just say it is not required (use `don't have to`)?

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `don't have to` for a prohibition: the learner thinks both mean `not allowed`
- Using `mustn't` for a missing obligation
- Using `do` with `must`, or `to` after `must`
- Writing `doesn't has to` or `don't has to`: after `does` the verb is `have`

**Register and usage** — `Mustn't` is strong and direct, often on signs. In speech people often say `can't` or `not allowed to`.
rules.llmDescription: Negative obligation: mustn't means forbidden, don't have to means not necessary; errors are swapped meanings, don't must, doesn't has to, do I must.

rules.title: May and might for possibility
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You use it to talk about uncertain plans and guesses.

**In simple words** — `may` / `might` + plain verb mean "maybe": `It may rain`, `I might go`. No `to` and no `-s` after them.

**The idea** — `may` and `might` say that something is possible but not sure. The speaker does not know. They are modal verbs, so they stay simple: one form, followed by a bare verb. `might` is a little less sure than `may`.

**The form**
- subject + `may` / `might` + base verb
- the same form for every person: no `-s`
- no `to` and no `-ing` after the modal
- negative: `may not` / `might not` + base verb
- question: asking about possibility is usually done with `Do you think ... might ...?`
- `maybe` (one word, adverb) goes at the start: no verb `be` needed after it
- `may be` (two words) = modal + verb `be`
- no `do` or `does` with these modals

**When it applies**
- Weather, plans and predictions you are not sure about
- Guesses about the present or the future; signal words: `perhaps`, `I'm not sure`, `I don't know`, `it's possible`
- Choices that are still open

**When it does NOT apply** — `will` and `be going to` express certainty or a firm plan. `can` expresses general ability or permission. Test: can the speaker say "maybe"? Use `may` or `might`. Does the speaker know it will happen? Use `will`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Adding `to` after the modal: the learner copies the pattern of normal verbs
- Adding `-s` after he, she, it
- Using `maybe` instead of `may be`, or using both together
- Using the past or `-ing` form after the modal
- Using `mayn't`: use `may not` or `might not`

**Register and usage** — `might` is common in everyday speech; `may` sounds a little more formal. The negative contraction `mightn't` is rare.
rules.llmDescription: Possibility with may, might + bare infinitive; maybe versus may be; errors are may to, mights, maybe as a verb, -ing or past form after the modal.

examples.correct: He may not know the answer.

rules.title: Enough and too
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You use it to complain, explain limits and describe things when shopping or choosing.

**In simple words** — `too` = more than is good: `too hot`. `enough` = as much as needed: `big enough`, `enough money`. `enough` goes after an adjective but before a noun.

**The idea** — `enough` and `too` describe the limit of an amount or a quality. `enough` means as much as needed; `too` means more than is good. Their position in the sentence is different, and learners often swap them or put them in the wrong place.

**The form**
- adjective or adverb + `enough`: `enough` comes after it
- `enough` + noun: `enough` comes before the noun
- `too` + adjective or adverb: `too` comes before it
- `too much` + uncountable noun; `too many` + countable plural noun
- `enough` / `too` + `to` + base verb: the result or purpose
- `too` + adjective + `for` + person + `to` + verb: someone else is the doer
- negative with `enough`: `not` + adjective + `enough` = too little
- never repeat the object pronoun after `to` + verb

**When it applies**
- Measuring a quality against a need: size, age, speed, temperature, price
- Counting amounts: time, money, chairs, food
- Explaining why something is impossible or possible; signal words: `can't`, `couldn't`, `so`

**When it does NOT apply** — `very` is a strong but neutral intensifier and does not suggest a result or a limit. `too` is negative; it always means a problem. Test: is there a problem or a limit? Use `too`. Is the amount sufficient? Use `enough`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Putting `enough` before an adjective: the learner copies the position of `too`
- Putting `enough` after a noun
- Using `too much` before an adjective: only `too` is needed
- Repeating the object after the infinitive
- Using `very` where `too` is needed

**Register and usage** — Neutral and very frequent in everyday talk.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `too` can also mean `also`, placed at the end

rules.title: Already, yet and still
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — These words show how something relates to time and expectations, so they are everywhere in everyday talk.

**In simple words** — `already` = earlier than expected. `yet` = until now, in questions and negatives. `still` = it continues: `He is still sleeping`.

**The idea** — These three adverbs show how an action relates to time and to our expectations. `already` says that something happened earlier than expected; `yet` asks or says that something expected has not happened up to now; `still` says that something continues. Each one has its own position and sentence type.

**The form**
- `already` + past participle, or between the auxiliary and the participle; also at the end for stress
- `already` is used in positive sentences and in surprised questions
- `yet` goes at the end of a negative sentence or a question
- `still` goes before the main verb, but after `be` and after the first auxiliary
- negative with `still`: `still` goes before `not` / `n't` for a surprise
- present perfect is typical with `already` and `yet`
- present simple or continuous is typical with `still`
- no `do` change: the adverbs do not affect the verb form

**When it applies**
- `already`: finished earlier than expected; signal: `so soon`, `by now`
- `yet`: waiting for something; signal: negatives and questions about results
- `still`: something goes on longer than expected; signal: `even now`, `after all this time`

**When it does NOT apply** — `yet` is not used in positive statements about the present; `still` is not used with a finished action. Test: is the action finished (`already` or `yet`) or does it continue (`still`)? In a positive sentence use `already`; in a negative or a question use `yet`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `already` in negatives instead of `yet`
- Using `yet` in a positive statement
- Putting `still` at the end of a sentence
- Using `still` with a finished action
- Putting `yet` before the verb

**Register and usage** — Neutral. In American English the past simple is also used with `already` and `yet`.

rules.title: Order of adjectives
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — It is a rule most native speakers follow without knowing it, and breaking it sounds unnatural.

**In simple words** — Opinion comes before fact: `a beautiful old wooden table`. General order: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material.

**The idea** — When several adjectives describe one noun, English does not let them come in any order. Native speakers follow a fixed pattern, from the speaker's opinion to the material of the thing. The order sounds natural even though most people cannot say the rule aloud.

**The form**
- 1. opinion: beautiful, nice, expensive
- 2. size: big, small, tall
- 3. age: old, new, young
- 4. shape: round, square, flat
- 5. colour: red, blue, black
- 6. origin: Italian, Chinese, German
- 7. material: wooden, silk, leather
- the article or possessive comes before all adjectives

**When it applies**
- Descriptions of objects, people, places and food
- Two or more adjectives before a noun

**When it does NOT apply** — Adjectives from the same group can swap: they are joined by `and` or a comma. Test: say the list from left to right: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, then the noun.

**Typical mistakes**
- Putting colour before size: the learner follows the order of thinking
- Putting material or origin before age or colour
- Putting the opinion adjective next to the noun
- Making the adjective plural to agree with the noun

**Register and usage** — Natural in speech and writing. More than three adjectives sounds heavy and is avoided.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- A noun used as an adjective stays directly before the main noun
rules.llmDescription: Order of several adjectives before a noun: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material; errors are colour, origin or material placed before size or age.

rules.title: Adjectives ending in -ed and -ing
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You use these to describe feelings, and "I'm boring" instead of "I'm bored" is a classic mistake.

**In simple words** — `-ing` describes what causes the feeling: `The film is boring`. `-ed` describes how you feel: `I am bored`.

**The idea** — Many adjectives come from verbs of feeling, and they exist in two forms. The `-ing` form describes the thing or the person that causes the feeling. The `-ed` form describes the person who has the feeling. Using the wrong one changes who is meant.

**The form**
- `-ing` adjective: the cause, the source of the feeling
- `-ed` adjective: the person (or animal) that feels
- both come after `be`, `feel`, `find`, `seem`, `look`, or before a noun
- no other ending: no plural, no agreement
- common pairs: bored and boring, interested and interesting, tired and tiring, excited and exciting, surprised and surprising, confused and confusing
- `-ed` adjectives are often followed by a preposition: `interested in`, `bored with`, `worried about`, `surprised at`
- after `-ing` adjectives there is usually no preposition
- negative and question forms are the normal ones for the verb `be`

**When it applies**
- Describing feelings: signal verbs such as `feel`, `be`, `get`
- Describing causes: films, books, lessons, news, jobs, trips, people

**When it does NOT apply** — An `-ed` form is also the past participle of a verb. In a verb phrase, such as the passive, it keeps its normal role. Test: is the word about a feeling inside a person? Use `-ed`. Is it about the thing that gives that feeling? Use `-ing`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `-ing` for the person who feels: the learner says what the person is, not what he feels
- Using `-ed` for the thing that causes the feeling
- Forgetting the usual preposition after `-ed` adjectives
- Adding an extra word (very, so) wrongly before a participle that works as a verb

**Register and usage** — Frequent in everyday talk. `very` is allowed with these adjectives; `much` is not.

rules.title: Stative verbs
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — Verbs like know, want and love are very common, and "I am wanting" is a typical mistake.

**In simple words** — Verbs of thinking, feeling and owning (`know`, `like`, `want`, `have`) are normally not used with `-ing`: `I know`, not "I am knowing".

**The idea** — Some verbs describe a state, not an action: what we think, feel, own or what something is. A state does not go on in steps, so these verbs do not normally appear in the continuous forms, even when the state is true now. The present simple is used instead.

**The form**
- stative verb + present simple: `know`, `knows`
- no `am` / `is` / `are` + `-ing` with these verbs
- negative: `do not` / `does not` + base verb
- question: `Do` / `Does` + subject + base verb
- verbs of thinking: know, understand, believe, remember, forget, think (opinion)
- verbs of feeling: like, love, hate, want, need, prefer
- verbs of possession and being: have (own), own, belong, contain, cost, mean
- verbs of the senses and appearance: seem, appear, sound, taste, smell, look (seem)

**When it applies**
- Present states, opinions and feelings
- The same rule in the past: use the simple form, not the past continuous
- Signal: the sentence describes a condition, not an event

**When it does NOT apply** — Some of these verbs have a second, active meaning and then can be continuous: `think` (consider), `have` (eat, take), `taste` (test), `see` (meet), `look` (watch). Test: can you replace the verb with `be` or `own`? Then it is a state and stays simple. If it describes an activity, the continuous is possible.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the continuous because the situation is happening now
- Using it for emotions such as `love` or `hate`
- Using it for `have` meaning own
- Copying a pattern from advertising slogans, where it is a special style

**Register and usage** — The continuous with `love` is used in informal speech for a new feeling, and in slogans. In learner English, avoid it.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `be` can be continuous when it describes behaviour: `being` + adjective
rules.llmDescription: State verbs (know, want, love, need, have for possession, seem) take the present simple, not the continuous; error is am/is/are + -ing with these verbs.

rules.title: No article in fixed expressions
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — Everyday phrases like go to school, at home and by bus follow this pattern.

**In simple words** — In many set phrases there is no article: `go to school`, `go to bed`, `at home`, `by bus`. Do not add `the` or `a` to these fixed phrases.

**The idea** — Some everyday words are used without an article because they name an activity or a purpose, not a particular building or object. When we say that someone goes to school, we mean that they study; we do not mean the building. Many such fixed expressions also use a preposition.

**The form**
- `go to` / `be at` / `be in` + bare place noun: school, work, bed, church, prison, hospital, university
- `go home` / `be at home`: no `to` with `home`, no article
- `by` + vehicle: by bus, by car, by train, by plane, by bike, by taxi
- `on foot`: also without article
- meals: `have breakfast`, `have lunch`, `have dinner`
- times of day: `at night`, `at noon`, `at midnight`; but `in the morning`, `in the evening`
- seasons and days of the week often have no article in general statements: in summer, on Monday
- with a specific building or a modifier, the article returns: `the school` of our town

**When it applies**
- Daily routines: school, work, bed, meals, transport
- Purpose rather than place: study, work, sleep, pray, be treated, serve a sentence

**When it does NOT apply** — When you mean the building itself, or one particular place, use the article. Test: do you think about the activity (no article) or the physical object or place (`the`)?

**Typical mistakes**
- Adding `the` to routine places: the learner treats them like ordinary nouns
- Adding `a` or `the` after `by` + vehicle
- Using `to` with `home`
- Using `in the night` instead of `at night`
- Adding an article to meals

**Register and usage** — Standard in all registers. British and American speakers differ with `hospital` and `university`, so learn the common fixed forms.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `in the evening` and `in the morning` keep `the`
- After a modifier the article returns: a good school, the same job

rules.title: Both, either and neither
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You use these words to talk about two people, things or options.

**In simple words** — `both` = A and B, `either` = one or the other, `neither` = not A and not B: `Both are good`, `Neither is free`.

**The idea** — These words talk about two things or two people. `both` means the two together; `either` means one of the two, it does not matter which; `neither` means none of the two. Each word has its own structure, and the verb agreement with them is a frequent problem.

**The form**
- `both` + plural noun, or `both of` + the / my / these + plural noun, with a plural verb
- `both ... and ...`: links two parts, with a plural verb for two subjects
- `either` + singular noun, or `either of` + plural, with a singular verb in formal use
- `either ... or ...`: offers a choice between two
- `neither` + singular noun, or `neither of` + plural, with a singular verb
- `neither ... nor ...`: negates both
- `neither` and `nor` already contain the negative: no extra `not`
- after a negative verb use `either`, not `neither`

**When it applies**
- Exactly two items: both hands, either side, neither parent
- Joining two nouns, adjectives or verbs with the paired word
- Short answers: `Neither.` `Either.` `Both.`

**When it does NOT apply** — For more than two, use `all`, `any` and `none`. Test: count the items. Two means this group of words; three or more means the other group.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using a singular verb with `both`
- Using a plural verb with `neither` or `either`
- Combining `neither` with a negative verb
- Using `both` with `or`, `either` with `and`, or `neither` with `or`
- Using `neither` and `nor` with a different grammatical form on each side

**Register and usage** — Neutral to formal. In speech the plural verb after `neither of` is common, but in writing the singular verb is preferred.
rules.llmDescription: Both, either, neither for two items: both + plural verb, either and neither + singular verb, both...and, either...or, neither...nor; errors are agreement, double negation, wrong pair.

rules.title: As ... as for equality
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You need it to say that two things are equal; it also appears in fixed phrases like "as soon as possible".

**In simple words** — `as` + adjective + `as`: `He is as tall as me`. Negative: `not as tall as`.

**The idea** — To say that two things are equal in some quality, English puts the adjective or adverb between two `as`. This is the comparison of equality. The structure is fixed: the first `as` is an adverb of degree, the second `as` introduces the thing we compare with.

**The form**
- `as` + adjective + `as`: equal quality
- `as` + adverb + `as`: equal way of doing
- negative: `not as` + adjective + `as`, or `not so` + adjective + `as`
- the adjective stays in the basic form: no `-er`, no `more`
- after the second `as` a noun, a pronoun or a clause can follow
- pronoun after the second `as`: `as tall as I am` (formal) or `as tall as me` (informal)
- `as much` / `as many` + noun + `as`: equal amount
- `the same ... as` is a neighbour pattern with the noun: same size, same age

**When it applies**
- Comparing people, objects, places, amounts
- Signal words: `just as`, `twice as`, `not quite as`, `almost as`
- Emphasis on equality or on a difference in degree

**When it does NOT apply** — The comparative with `-er` / `more` + `than` shows inequality; `as ... as` shows equality. Test: are the things unequal (use `than`) or equal (use `as ... as`)?

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `than` instead of the second `as`: the learner copies the comparative
- Using `like` instead of the second `as`
- Putting a comparative form between the two `as`
- Using `that` instead of `as` for a clause
- Using `good` instead of `well` as an adverb of manner

**Register and usage** — Neutral. `Not so ... as` is a little more formal and old-fashioned.
rules.llmDescription: Equality comparison as + adjective or adverb + as, not as ... as; errors are than, like or that instead of the second as, comparative between the two as.

examples.note: Use the basic form after as.

rules.title: Be able to for ability
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — It fills the gaps where `can` does not work, such as the future.

**In simple words** — `be able to` means the same as `can`: `I will be able to help you tomorrow`. Use it when `can` has no suitable form.

**The idea** — `can` has only two forms, present and a past form `could`. For all the other situations, such as the future, the present perfect or after another verb, English uses `be able to`. It is an ordinary phrase, built on the verb `be`, and means the same thing: having the ability or the chance to do something.

**The form**
- `be` + `able to` + base verb
- `be` takes the correct form for the subject and the tense: am, is, are, was, were, been, being
- future: `will be able to` + base verb
- present perfect: `have` / `has been able to` + base verb
- infinitive: `to be able to` + base verb, after verbs such as want, hope, need
- negative: `not able to` / `unable to`, with the right form of `be`
- question: the form of `be` + subject + `able to` + base verb
- `to` is part of the phrase, and the verb after it has no ending

**When it applies**
- Ability in tenses where `can` does not exist: future, perfect, infinitive, after a modal
- A single success in the past: `was able to` for one particular occasion
- Signal words: `after the course`, `by next year`, `so far`, `at last`

**When it does NOT apply** — In the present, `can` is shorter and more natural. For general past ability `could` is natural. Test: is `can` or `could` possible in this tense? If not, use `be able to`. For one specific success in the past, `was able to` is safer than `could`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `can` after another modal or `to`: `will can`, `to can`
- Using `can` in the present perfect
- Forgetting the form of `be`: `didn't able to`
- Leaving out `to`, or adding `-ing` or `-ed` after it

**Register and usage** — `be able to` sounds a little more formal than `can`. `unable to` is formal and typical of writing.
rules.llmDescription: Be able to where can has no form: will be able to, has been able to, to be able to; errors are will can, to can, missing be, missing to.

examples.correct: They are able to swim.
examples.note: After able to, use the base verb.

rules.title: Reflexive pronouns
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You use them in common phrases like "enjoy yourself", "introduce myself", "hurt himself".

**In simple words** — `myself`, `yourself`, `himself`, `herself`, `itself`, `ourselves`, `themselves` show the doer and the receiver are the same person: `I cut myself`. They can also add emphasis: `I did it myself`.

**The idea** — A reflexive pronoun shows that the person who does the action also receives it. Most English verbs need an object, and when the doer and the object are the same person, a normal object pronoun would point to someone else. The same words can also add emphasis or mean "alone": `by myself` means without help or company.

**The form**
- singular: `myself`, `yourself`, `himself`, `herself`, `itself`
- plural: `ourselves`, `yourselves`, `themselves`
- the pronoun matches the subject in person and number
- position: after the verb as its object, or after a preposition: `to herself`, `about themselves`
- `by` + reflexive pronoun = alone, without help
- negatives and questions keep the same pronoun: `didn't hurt himself`, `did you enjoy yourselves`

**When it applies**
- Doer and object are the same: `cut`, `hurt`, `burn`, `introduce`, `teach`, `blame`
- Fixed phrases: `enjoy yourself`, `help yourself`, `behave yourself`, `make yourself at home`
- Doing something alone: `by myself`, `by themselves`

**When it does NOT apply** — `each other` shows a two-way action between people. Test: does each person act on himself, or on the other one? Himself → `themselves`; the other one → `each other`. Many verbs that are reflexive in other languages are not reflexive in English: `relax`, `feel`, `meet`, `wash`, `dress`, `concentrate`, `wake up`.

**Typical mistakes**
- `hisself`, `theirselves`: built from the possessive word; the correct forms use `him` and `them`
- `-self` with a plural subject instead of `-selves`
- `themselves` for a two-way action instead of `each other`
- A reflexive after `relax`, `feel`, `meet`: copied from the learner's own language
- `myself` as a subject, or after `and` instead of `I` / `me`
- `enjoy` with no object: `enjoy` always needs one

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- After place prepositions use the object pronoun: `behind me`, `next to him`
- `yourself` is for one person, `yourselves` for several, although `you` is the same
rules.llmDescription: Reflexive pronouns myself, yourself, himself, ourselves, themselves for a doer acting on itself: hisself, themself, plural -self, themselves for each other, reflexive after relax, feel, meet.

rules.title: Look, sound, seem + adjective
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You use it to describe impressions: how things look, sound, feel and taste.

**In simple words** — After `look`, `sound`, `feel`, `seem`, `taste`, `smell` use an adjective, not an adverb: `You look tired`, `It smells good`.

**The idea** — Some verbs do not describe an action; they describe how something appears or feels to us. After these linking verbs English uses an adjective, because the word describes the subject, not the way an action is done. Learners who have just learnt -ly adverbs often add -ly here by mistake.

**The form**
- subject + linking verb + adjective
- verbs of the senses: `look`, `sound`, `smell`, `taste`, `feel`
- other linking verbs: `seem`, `appear`, `become`, `get`, `stay`, `remain`
- linking verb + `like` + noun: `look like a model`, `sound like a plan`
- with a degree word: `look really tired`, `seem a bit strange`
- negative: `doesn't look`, `didn't sound`; question: `does it taste`, `do I look`
- -s on the linking verb with he, she, it and singular nouns

**When it applies**
- First impressions of people, food, music, ideas
- Reactions to what you see, hear, smell, taste or touch
- Changes of state with `get`, `become`, `stay`: `get angry`, `stay calm`

**When it does NOT apply** — If the same verb is a real action, it takes an adverb: `look carefully at`, `taste the soup slowly`, `feel the wall gently` (see adverbs of manner with -ly). Test: can you replace the verb with `is`? If yes, use an adjective; if not, it is an action and needs an adverb.

**Typical mistakes**
- -ly after a linking verb: `look tiredly`, `sound nicely`, copied from action verbs
- No `like` before a noun: `look a doctor`
- `like` before an adjective: `look like tired`
- `smell badly` instead of `smell bad`
- An adverb after `get`, `become` or `stay`: `got angrily`, `stay calmly`

**Register and usage** — Everyday spoken English; `appear` and `remain` are more formal. Short reactions like `sounds good`, `looks great` are extremely frequent.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `good` is the adjective and `well` the adverb, but `well` is also an adjective meaning healthy: `feel well`
rules.llmDescription: Linking verbs look, sound, seem, smell, taste, feel, get, stay + adjective or like + noun: -ly adverb after them, like before an adjective, missing like before a noun.

rules.title: Other, another and others
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You need these words every time you talk about more, different or remaining things.

**In simple words** — `another` = one more (`another cup`). `other` goes before a noun (`the other day`). `others` stands alone, with no noun.

**The idea** — These words talk about something different or additional. `another` means one more or a different one; `other` describes a noun; `others` stands alone without a noun. Learners mix them because their own language often has one word for all of them.

**The form**
- `another` + singular countable noun; it is `an` + `other` written as one word
- `another` + number + plural noun: an extra amount, `another two days`
- `other` + plural or uncountable noun: `other people`, `other music`
- `the other` + singular noun: the second of two, or the last one
- `the other` + plural noun: the rest of a known group
- `others`: a pronoun, plural, with no noun after it
- `the others`: the rest of a known group, no noun after it
- `other` before a noun never takes -s: it is an adjective

**When it applies**
- One more of the same: another coffee, another try
- A different one: another day, another colour
- The rest of a group: the others, the other students
- Two sides: `one ... the other`, `some ... others`

**When it does NOT apply** — `more` gives an extra amount of uncountable things or plurals: `more water`, `more chairs`. `another` is for one countable thing. Test: one countable thing extra → `another`; an amount → `more`.

**Typical mistakes**
- `an other` written as two words
- `another` with a plural noun: `another books`
- `others` before a noun: the -s is copied from the noun
- `the another`: `another` already contains `an`
- `another` with an uncountable noun instead of `more`

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `the other day` is a fixed phrase meaning a few days ago
- `each other` is a pronoun for a two-way action, not part of this choice

rules.title: Each, every and all
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — They are very common words for whole groups, and the verb after them often causes mistakes.

**In simple words** — `every` and `each` + singular noun + singular verb: `Every student has a book`. `all` + plural: `All students have books`.

**The idea** — All three talk about a whole group, but in different ways. `every` sees the group as a whole made of single members; `each` looks at the members one by one; `all` takes the group together. The grammar after each word is different, and that is where the mistakes happen.

**The form**
- `every` + singular countable noun + singular verb
- `each` + singular countable noun + singular verb
- `each of` / `every one of` + `the`, `my`, `these` + plural noun, singular verb in careful use
- `each` can follow a plural subject: `they each have`, the verb agrees with the subject
- `every` cannot stand alone and has no `every of`
- `all` + plural noun + plural verb, or `all` + uncountable noun + singular verb
- `all of` + `the` / `my` + noun; `all of` + pronoun: `all of us`
- `everyone`, `everything`, `everybody` take a singular verb

**When it applies**
- A whole group or a routine: every week, every time, every student
- Members seen separately, often a small number: each side, each child
- Totals: all the money, all my friends

**When it does NOT apply** — For exactly two, use `both` (see both, either and neither). `each` works for two, `every` needs three or more. Test: one by one → `each`; whole group seen as single members → `every`; the group together with a plural verb → `all`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Plural noun after `every` or `each`: copied from the plural meaning
- Plural verb after `every`, `each of` or `everyone`
- `every of`: use `each of` or `every one of`
- `all days` or `all day` for a repeated routine: say `every day`
- `all` + singular countable noun: `all student`
- `all of` + noun without `the` or `my`

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `every` with numbers: every two weeks, every few days
- `all day` means the whole day, `every day` means each day repeatedly
rules.llmDescription: Every and each + singular noun and verb, each of + plural, no every of, all + plural noun, every day versus all day; plural after every, everyone are.

examples.correct: Every student has a laptop.

rules.title: Most and most of
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — It lets you say "the majority" correctly, in general or about a specific group.

**In simple words** — `most people` (in general) but `most of the people` (a specific group, with `the`, `my`, `these`).

**The idea** — `most` means the biggest part of a group or an amount. English separates two ideas: people or things in general, and a known, specific group. The word `of` together with `the`, `my`, `these` shows that the group is specific.

**The form**
- `most` + plural or uncountable noun: general meaning, no article, no `of`
- `most of` + `the` / `my` / `these` / `our` + noun: a specific group
- `most of` + object pronoun: `most of them`, `most of us`
- `most` alone as a pronoun when the noun is clear
- the verb agrees with the noun: plural noun → plural verb, uncountable → singular

**When it applies**
- Generalisations: most people, most children, most food
- Statements about a known group: most of my colleagues, most of the time
- Results and statistics: most of the students, most of the money

**When it does NOT apply** — `the most` is the superlative: `the most expensive`, `who ate the most` (see superlative adjectives). Test: does it mean the majority? Use `most` or `most of`, without `the` in front. Does it compare with others? Use `the most`.

**Typical mistakes**
- `most of people`: `of` without `the` or `my` before the noun
- `the most people` meaning the majority: the article is copied from the superlative
- `most the`, `most my`: `of` is missing
- `most of` + subject pronoun: `most of they`
- `the most of` meaning the majority
- `mostly` or `almost` used as a quantifier before a noun

**Register and usage** — Neutral and very frequent in speech and writing.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `most of the time` and `for the most part` are fixed phrases
- `almost all` is close in meaning to `most`; `almost` alone is an adverb
- `mostly` means mainly and goes before a verb or adjective
rules.llmDescription: Majority quantifier most + noun in general, most of + the, my or pronoun for a specific group: most of people, the most people, most the, mostly.

examples.correct: Most people like summer.
examples.note: For people in general, drop of.

examples.correct: Most students passed the exam.
examples.note: No the when meaning the majority.

examples.note: Mostly is an adverb, not a quantifier.

examples.note: Almost is not a quantifier; use most.

examples.note: A specific group needs the after of.

examples.wrong: Most of the guests wasn't happy with the hotel.
examples.correct: Most of the guests weren't happy with the hotel.
examples.note: A plural noun needs a plural verb.

rules.title: Adjectives with prepositions
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — Many everyday adjectives need a particular preposition, and it is often different in your own language.

**In simple words** — Learn the adjective together with its preposition: `good at`, `afraid of`, `interested in`, `proud of`.

**The idea** — Many adjectives join a noun, a pronoun or an -ing form with one fixed preposition: `good at`, `afraid of`, `interested in`. The preposition does not follow logic and is often different in the learner's own language, so it has to be learnt together with the adjective.

**The form**
- adjective + preposition + noun or pronoun
- adjective + preposition + verb-ing, never `to` + verb after the preposition
- abilities: `good at`, `bad at`, `brilliant at`
- feelings: `afraid of`, `scared of`, `proud of`, `tired of`, `fond of`
- interest: `interested in`, `keen on`, `crazy about`, `excited about`, `worried about`
- anger: `angry with` a person, `angry about` a situation
- relations: `married to`, `kind to`, `similar to`, `different from`
- others: `full of`, `famous for`, `responsible for`, `ready for`
- in questions the preposition stays at the end: `what are you afraid of`

**When it applies**
- Talking about skills, fears, interests and emotions
- Describing people and their relations to others
- Whenever a thing or activity follows the adjective

**When it does NOT apply** — Verbs have their own prepositions (`depend on`, `listen to`): that is a separate list of verb patterns. For feeling adjectives, first choose `-ed` or `-ing` (see adjectives ending in -ed and -ing), then the preposition. Test: is the word before the preposition an adjective after `be`, `feel`, `get`? Then use this list.

**Typical mistakes**
- Translating the preposition: `afraid from`, `married with`, `interested about`
- `good in` instead of `good at` for skills
- A base verb after the preposition instead of -ing
- No preposition at all: `responsible the project`
- `angry on` instead of `angry with`

**Register and usage** — Very frequent in everyday talk about likes, fears and abilities. `different than` is common in American speech; `different from` is the safe choice.
rules.llmDescription: Fixed adjective + preposition pairs good at, afraid of, interested in, keen on, married to, famous for, then noun or -ing: wrong or missing preposition, to + verb.

examples.correct: I'm really keen on learning to surf.

examples.note: Use angry with for a person.

examples.correct: Who is responsible for the new project?

rules.title: Present perfect with just
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You use it to share fresh news: "I've just arrived".

**In simple words** — `have/has` + `just` + past participle: `I have just arrived`. It means a very short time ago.

**The idea** — `just` with the present perfect tells news: something happened a very short time ago and its result is fresh now. The speaker connects a very recent action with the present moment, so British English uses the present perfect here, not the past simple.

**The form**
- `have` / `has` + `just` + past participle
- `just` goes between the auxiliary and the participle
- contractions: `I've just`, `she's just`, `they've just`
- question: `Have` / `Has` + subject + `just` + participle
- `has` with he, she, it and singular nouns, `have` with the others
- past participle: regular -ed, or the third form of an irregular verb

**When it applies**
- Fresh news: a message, an arrival, a result
- Explaining what you see now by a very recent action: wet hair, an empty plate
- Announcements and surprises: `Look!`, `Guess what`

**When it does NOT apply** — With a finished time phrase (`a minute ago`, `at five`, `just now`) use the past simple (see past simple or present perfect). `just now` means a moment ago and takes the past simple. Test: is there a finished time phrase? Past simple. Fresh news without a time? `have just` + participle.

**Typical mistakes**
- `just` before `have`: copied from the position of frequency adverbs
- `just` after the participle
- The past form instead of the participle: `have just went`
- No auxiliary and a base verb: `she just arrive`
- Present perfect with `just now` or `ago`
- `is` or `are` instead of `has` / `have`: copied from the passive

**Register and usage** — In American speech the past simple with `just` is also normal; the present perfect is correct everywhere.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `just` also means only or simply; that is a different meaning
- `has just been` (and is back) differs from `has just gone` (and is still away)
rules.llmDescription: Recent news with have or has + just + past participle: just before have or after the participle, past form instead, missing have, just now or ago.

examples.correct: I have just finished my report.

examples.correct: She's just gone out to the shop.

examples.note: The present perfect uses has, not is.

examples.correct: We have just cleaned the kitchen floor.
examples.note: Just goes between have and the participle.

rules.title: Present simple for timetables
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You need it to talk about trains, flights, films and other fixed schedules.

**In simple words** — For fixed timetables use the present simple: `The train leaves at 6`, `The film starts at 8`.

**The idea** — English uses the present simple for future events fixed by a timetable, a programme or a calendar. The speaker sees the event as a fact that nobody can easily change, like the departure of a train, so a present form is enough to talk about the future.

**The form**
- subject + present simple + future time: `leaves at six`, `starts tomorrow`
- -s / -es with he, she, it and singular nouns: `the bus leaves`
- negative: `don't` / `doesn't` + base verb
- question: `What time` / `When` + `does` + singular subject + base verb; `do` + plural subject
- typical verbs: `leave`, `arrive`, `start`, `begin`, `finish`, `open`, `close`, `take off`, `land`
- a future time phrase is usually present: `at 7.30`, `on Monday`, `next week`

**When it applies**
- Transport timetables: trains, flights, buses, ferries
- Opening hours of shops, museums, banks
- Programmes and schedules: lessons, concerts, films, terms, matches

**When it does NOT apply** — Personal plans take the present continuous or `going to`; predictions take `will` (see going to for plans, will for decisions and predictions). Test: is the event fixed by an official timetable for everyone? Present simple. Is it a person's own plan? Present continuous or `going to`.

**Typical mistakes**
- No -s with a singular subject: the learner thinks "future" and drops the ending
- -s kept after `does` or `doesn't`
- `don't` with a singular subject, `does` with a plural one
- Statement order in a question, or the verb before the subject
- The present simple for a personal plan instead of the present continuous

**Register and usage** — Very frequent in travel, work and school talk, in announcements and emails.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `will` is also possible with a timetable, but the present simple is more natural
- after `when`, `until`, `as soon as` the present simple is required (see present tense in future time clauses)
rules.llmDescription: Present simple for future timetabled events leave, arrive, start, open, close at a time: missing -s, does + -s, wrong question order, don't with a singular subject.

rules.title: For, during and while
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — They are very frequent and easy to mix up when you say how long or when something happened.

**In simple words** — `for` + length of time (`for two hours`), `during` + event (`during the film`), `while` + clause (`while I was sleeping`).

**The idea** — All three connect an action with a period of time, but they answer different questions. `for` says how long; `during` says when, inside which event or period; `while` means the same as `during` but introduces a whole clause with a verb.

**The form**
- `for` + length of time: `for two hours`, `for a week`, `for ages`
- `during` + noun: `during the film`, `during the summer`, `during my stay`
- `while` + subject + verb: `while I was cooking`, `while she sleeps`
- `while` + -ing when the subject is the same: `while driving`
- `during` never takes a subject and verb after it
- `for` works with any tense
- `while` often takes the past continuous for a background action

**When it applies**
- How long: `for` + number + time word
- At some point within an event: `during` + the event (the meeting, the night, the holiday)
- Two things at the same time: `while` + clause

**When it does NOT apply** — With the present perfect and a starting point, use `since` (see present perfect with for and since). Test: does the answer say how long? → `for`. Does it name an event or period? → `during`. Does a subject and verb or an -ing form follow? → `while`.

**Typical mistakes**
- `during` + length of time: `during two hours`, copied from a one-word translation
- `during` + clause: `during I was sleeping`
- `during` + -ing: `during playing`
- `while` + noun: `while the lesson`
- `for` + event noun meaning "at some point in it"

**Register and usage** — All three are neutral. `during` is a little more frequent in writing.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `for` can be dropped in speech after some verbs: `wait an hour`
- `meanwhile` is an adverb, not a preposition: it starts a new clause
rules.llmDescription: For + length of time, during + event or period noun, while + clause or -ing: during two hours, during I was, while the film, for meaning when.

examples.correct: I lived in Spain for three years.

examples.correct: Someone called while I was in the shower.

examples.correct: Please don't talk during the film.

rules.title: Until and by for deadlines
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — Mixing them can change the whole meaning of a deadline or an arrangement.

**In simple words** — `until` = continues up to that time: `I'll wait until 5`. `by` = not later than that time: `Finish it by 5`.

**The idea** — Both words look at a point in time, but they say different things. `until` means an action or state continues up to that point and then stops. `by` means something happens before that point at the latest: it is a deadline. Choosing the wrong word changes the meaning.

**The form**
- `until` / `till` + time point: an action or state continues up to then
- `by` + time point: not later than; the action is complete
- `until` + clause: present simple for the future, never `will`
- `by the time` + clause: a deadline expressed with a verb
- `not ... until` + time: the action starts only at that point
- `by` often goes with `have to`, `must`, `need to` and the future perfect
- `till` is informal; `up until` is spoken

**When it applies**
- Duration up to a point: wait, stay, work, sleep, keep, be open + `until`
- Deadlines: finish, send, pay, return, check out + `by`
- Delays: `not until` = only then

**When it does NOT apply** — `by` does not go with verbs of duration (`wait`, `stay`, `keep`), and `until` does not mark a deadline for a one-time action (`finish`, `send`, `pay`). Test: can you add "all the time up to then"? → `until`. Can you add "at the latest"? → `by`. For the tense after `until` see present tense in future time clauses.

**Typical mistakes**
- `until` for a deadline: copied from a language where one word means both
- `by` for a continuing action or state
- `to` instead of `until` after a duration verb: `stay to noon`
- `will` in a clause after `until`
- `by` + clause instead of `by the time` + clause

**Register and usage** — Very frequent at work, in school and in emails about deadlines.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `from ... to ...` and `from ... until ...` are both correct for a period
- `by now`, `by then` mean already at this or that moment
rules.llmDescription: Until for a state lasting up to a point (wait, stay, open), by for a deadline (finish, send, pay): swapped words, by + clause, will after until.

rules.title: Hard, hardly, late and lately
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — Pairs like hard/hardly and late/lately look similar but mean very different things.

**In simple words** — `hard` = with effort (`work hard`), `hardly` = almost not (`hardly sleep`), `late` = not on time, `lately` = recently.

**The idea** — Most adverbs are made with -ly, but a few common words have the same form as the adjective: `hard`, `late`, `fast`, `early`, `near`, `high`. Adding -ly to some of them creates a different word with a different meaning: `hardly` means almost not, `lately` means recently. The wrong form changes the meaning of the sentence.

**The form**
- `hard` = adjective and adverb: with great effort (`work hard`, `try hard`)
- `hardly` = almost not; before the main verb, after `be` and auxiliaries
- `hardly` + `any`, `ever`, `anyone`: `hardly any time`, `hardly ever`
- `late` = adjective and adverb: not on time (`arrive late`, `stay up late`)
- `lately` = recently; usually with the present perfect, at the end
- `fast`, `early`, `daily` = adjective and adverb, no -ly form exists
- `near` = close; `nearly` = almost
- `high` = at a high level; `highly` = very much (`highly recommended`)
- `hardly` is already negative: no `not` or `never` with it

**When it applies**
- Effort, speed, time: work hard, drive fast, get up early, come late
- Almost nothing: hardly know, hardly any money
- A recent period: lately, with `have` + participle

**When it does NOT apply** — For ordinary adjectives the -ly rule works normally (see adverbs of manner with -ly). Test: is the word in this short list? Then check the meaning: effort or not on time → no -ly; almost not or recently → -ly.

**Typical mistakes**
- `work hardly` meaning with effort: the regular -ly rule is overgeneralised and the meaning becomes "almost not"
- `come lately` meaning not on time
- `fastly`, `earlily`: these words do not exist
- `can't hardly`: double negative
- `hardly` after the main verb, or before a noun without `any`

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `hardly` at the start of a sentence with inversion is formal (see inversion after negative adverbials)
rules.llmDescription: Flat adverbs hard, late, fast, early, near, high versus -ly words with another meaning hardly, lately, nearly, highly: work hardly, come lately, fastly, can't hardly, hardly without any.

rules.title: The -ing form as subject
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You need it when an activity is the topic: "Swimming is fun".

**In simple words** — To make an activity the subject, use `-ing`: `Swimming is fun`. Not "Swim is fun".

**The idea** — When an activity itself is the topic of a sentence, English names it with the -ing form, which works like a noun. A bare verb cannot be the subject, so learners who translate word for word often start the sentence with the base form.

**The form**
- verb-ing (+ object or place) as the subject: `swimming`, `learning languages`, `living alone`
- one -ing subject takes a singular verb: `is`, `helps`, `makes`, even with a plural noun inside the phrase
- negative subject: `not` + verb-ing
- question: `is` / `does` + verb-ing phrase
- alternative with the same meaning: `it is` + adjective + `to` + base verb
- with `it is` + adjective, `it` is required and `to` comes before the verb
- two -ing subjects joined by `and` take a plural verb

**When it applies**
- Opinions about activities: easy, fun, healthy, dangerous, expensive
- Rules and signs: smoking, parking, camping
- Statements about hobbies, habits and health

**When it does NOT apply** — After certain verbs and prepositions the -ing form is an object (see verb plus -ing form). Here the -ing form starts the sentence and is the subject. Test: does the activity come first, before the main verb? Use verb-ing, or move it to the end with `it is ... to`.

**Typical mistakes**
- A bare verb as subject: copied from a word-for-word translation
- A plural verb because the phrase contains a plural noun: `learning words are`
- No `it` before `is` + adjective + `to`
- No `to` after `it is` + adjective
- A bare verb after `not` at the start

**Register and usage** — Everyday and neutral. `To` + verb as a subject exists but is formal and rare; in speech prefer -ing or `it is ... to`.
rules.llmDescription: Activity as sentence subject with verb-ing (swimming is, learning words is) or it is + adjective + to: bare verb as subject, plural verb after an -ing subject, missing it.

examples.note: Use the -ing form as a subject.

examples.correct: It is important to drink enough water.

rules.title: Verbs with two objects
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — Verbs like give, send, show and buy are used every day with two objects.

**In simple words** — You can say `give her a book` or `give a book to her`. Person first = no `to`; thing first = with `to`.

**The idea** — Some verbs have two objects: the thing that is given or made, and the person who receives it. English allows two orders, but each order has its own rules, and some verbs that look similar allow only one order.

**The form**
- verb + person + thing: `give me the keys`, `send her a message`
- verb + thing + `to` / `for` + person: `give the keys to me`
- `to` with transfer verbs: `give`, `send`, `lend`, `show`, `offer`, `pay`, `sell`, `teach`, `bring`
- `for` with verbs of doing something for someone: `buy`, `make`, `cook`, `get`, `find`, `book`
- in the first order, no preposition before the person
- `explain`, `describe`, `suggest`, `introduce`, `report`: only verb + thing + `to` + person
- a pronoun thing (`it`, `them`) usually goes first: verb + `it` + `to` / `for` + person

**When it applies**
- Giving, sending, showing, lending, paying something to someone
- Buying, cooking, finding, booking something for someone
- Requests: `can you lend me`, `could you pass me`

**When it does NOT apply** — `tell` / `ask` + person + `to` + verb reports a command (see reported commands and requests), not a thing given. Test: is the second object a thing? This rule. Is it an action? The infinitive pattern.

**Typical mistakes**
- `explain me`, `describe us`, `suggest me`: copied from `give` and `tell`
- `to` in the first order: `give to me the keys`
- `for` with transfer verbs, or `to` with `buy`, `get`, `cook`
- Thing first but no `to` before the person: `give the money me`
- `introduce` + person + person in the wrong order

**Register and usage** — Very frequent. The person-first order is more common in speech; the new or important information goes last.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `give me it` and `give it me` are heard in British speech, but `give it to me` is the safe choice
rules.llmDescription: Two-object verbs give, send, show, offer, buy, cook: person + thing or thing + to/for + person; explain, describe, suggest only thing + to + person.

rules.title: Make, let and help + object
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — These verbs are very common, and adding `to` after them is a typical mistake.

**In simple words** — `make` and `let` + person + plain verb, no `to`: `She made me wait`, `Let me go`. After `help` `to` is optional.

**The idea** — `make` means to force or cause someone to do something, `let` means to allow it, and `help` means to assist. After these verbs and their object, English uses the base verb without `to`. Learners add `to` because most verbs with a similar meaning (`want`, `ask`, `allow`) take it.

**The form**
- `make` + object + base verb: force or cause
- `let` + object + base verb: allow
- `help` + object + base verb or `to` + verb: both correct
- negative: `didn't make`, `don't let`; question: `did they make you`, `will you let me`
- `let` has the same form in present, past and participle; past of `make` is `made`
- passive of `make` brings back `to`: `be made to` + verb
- `let` has no passive: use `be allowed to`
- `make` + object + adjective: `make me happy`

**When it applies**
- Rules and pressure from parents, teachers, bosses
- Permission: `let me`, `let us`, `let them`
- Feelings caused by something: `made me cry`, `makes me laugh`
- Offers: `let me help`, `let me know`

**When it does NOT apply** — `allow`, `force`, `ask`, `want`, `get` take object + `to` + verb (see verb plus to-infinitive). `let's` + base verb is a suggestion (see imperatives and let's), not permission. Test: is the verb `make` or `let` in the active? No `to`. Any other verb with this meaning? Add `to`.

**Typical mistakes**
- `to` after `make` or `let` + object: copied from `allow` and `want`
- -ing after the object: `made me waiting`
- Past or -s form after the object: `let them watched`
- `letted` as the past form
- Active pattern in the passive: `was made clean` instead of `was made to clean`
- `let` in the passive instead of `be allowed to`

**Register and usage** — Everyday, especially when talking about family, school and work.
rules.llmDescription: Make and let + object + bare infinitive, help + object + base verb or to: to after make or let, -ing after object, letted, passive be made to.

rules.title: Making suggestions
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You use it to suggest plans to friends and colleagues.

**In simple words** — Common ways: `Let's go`, `Why don't we go?`, `How about going?`, `We could go`, `I suggest going`. Each one needs a different verb form after it.

**The idea** — When we suggest an activity, English uses a few fixed patterns. Each pattern requires its own verb form after it, and this is where learners go wrong: they put `to` + verb or a base verb where -ing is needed, or the other way round.

**The form**
- `Shall we` + base verb: asking for agreement on a joint plan
- `Shall I` + base verb: an offer
- `Let's` + base verb; negative `Let's not` + base verb
- `How about` / `What about` + verb-ing or noun
- `Why don't we` / `Why don't you` + base verb, in question order
- `We could` + base verb: a softer suggestion
- `Do you fancy` / `Do you feel like` + verb-ing or noun, informal
- answers: `Good idea`, `Why not`, `I'd rather not`

**When it applies**
- Planning free time, trips, food, meetings
- Friendly advice to someone: `why don't you`
- Offering to do something for someone: `shall I`

**When it does NOT apply** — The verb `suggest` itself has its own patterns and is more formal. `should` gives advice, not a joint plan (see should for advice). Test: are you proposing an idea to do together or offering help? Use these fixed patterns.

**Typical mistakes**
- `to` + verb or a base verb after `how about`: `about` is a preposition, so only -ing or a noun
- `Why we don't`: statement order instead of question order
- `to` after `shall`, `could` or `don't we`
- -ing after `shall`: `shall I opening`
- `Let's don't`: the negative is `let's not`
- `to` after `fancy` or `feel like`

**Register and usage** — `Shall we` is mainly British; Americans prefer `Should we` or `Do you want to`. `Do you fancy` is informal British.
rules.llmDescription: Suggestions: shall we + base verb, how about + -ing, why don't we + base verb, let's not, fancy + -ing; errors: to added, why we don't.

rules.title: Had better for strong advice
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You use it to give strong advice or a warning.

**In simple words** — `You'd better go` = you should, or something bad may happen. Use a plain verb. Negative: `had better not`.

**The idea** — `had better` gives strong advice about the present or near future, often with a warning: if you don't do it, something bad will happen. Although it contains `had`, it does not talk about the past.

**The form**
- subject + `had better` + base verb
- contracted: `I'd better`, `you'd better`, `she'd better`
- the same form for all persons: never `has better`, no -s on the verb
- negative: `had better not` + base verb
- question is rare: `Had I better` + base verb; `Should I` is more usual
- no `to` after `better`, and none after `not`
- time: now or the near future, often with `now`, `tonight`, `or`, `otherwise`

**When it applies**
- Urgent advice with a risk: weather, health, money, being late
- Warnings and threats with `or` or `otherwise`
- Advice to yourself: `I'd better go`

**When it does NOT apply** — `should` is general advice or opinion without a warning (see should for advice). `would rather` is preference, not advice (see would rather and it's time). Test: is there a clear bad result here and now if the advice is ignored? `had better`. A general opinion? `should`.

**Typical mistakes**
- `to` after `better`: copied from `have to` and `ought to`
- `has better` with he, she or a singular noun: `had` never changes
- -ing, past or -s form instead of the base verb
- `not` before `better` instead of after it
- `'d` read as `would`: `would better`
- `don't had better` as a negative

**Register and usage** — Mostly spoken; it can sound like an order, so avoid it with a boss or strangers. In fast informal speech `had` almost disappears.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- it never gives advice about the past; for past criticism see should have and ought to have
rules.llmDescription: Had better or 'd better + bare infinitive for urgent advice, negative had better not: to after better, has better, would better, -s or -ing on the verb.

rules.title: Reported commands and requests
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You need it to say what people told or asked you to do.

**In simple words** — `He told me to wait`, `She asked me not to be late`: told/asked + person + (not) to + verb.

**The idea** — When we report what someone told or asked us to do, English does not repeat the imperative. It uses a reporting verb, the person, and `to` + verb. This is shorter and clearer than repeating the exact words.

**The form**
- `tell` / `ask` + object + `to` + base verb
- negative: `tell` / `ask` + object + `not to` + base verb
- the same pattern: `order`, `warn`, `remind`, `advise`, `beg`, `invite`, `encourage`
- the person comes directly after the verb, without `to`
- pronouns change to fit the reporter: `your` → `my`, `me` → `him`
- no backshift: the infinitive has no tense
- `say` cannot take object + `to` + verb; use `tell` or `ask`

**When it applies**
- Reporting orders, instructions, warnings, advice
- Reporting polite requests with `Could you`, `Please`
- Reporting invitations and reminders

**When it does NOT apply** — Reported statements use `that` + clause with backshift (see reported statements and backshift); reported questions use `if` or a wh-word + statement order (see reported questions). Test: was the original an imperative or a request to act? → object + `to` + verb. Was it information? → `that` + clause.

**Typical mistakes**
- `that` + clause instead of object + `to`: copied from reported statements
- `don't` instead of `not to`: the imperative is kept
- `not` without `to`: `told me not leave`
- No `to` before the verb: `asked me help`
- `said me to`: `say` used like `tell`
- `to` before the person: `told to me`
- -ing instead of `to` + verb

**Register and usage** — Very common in stories, messages and at work; `order` and `beg` are strong, `remind` and `invite` neutral.
rules.llmDescription: Reported commands and requests tell, ask, order, warn, remind, advise + object + (not) to + verb: that-clause, don't, missing to, said me to, to before the person, -ing.

examples.correct: Did your boss tell you to finish it today?

examples.correct: He told me to wait outside.

rules.title: A friend of mine
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — It is the natural way to say "one of my friends".

**In simple words** — `a friend of mine`, `a colleague of hers`. Not "a my friend".

**The idea** — When we talk about one person or thing from a group that belongs to someone, English uses `a` + noun + `of` + possessive pronoun. It shows that there are others too, and that this one is new to the listener. English cannot put `a` and `my` together, so it needs this special pattern.

**The form**
- `a` / `an` + noun + `of` + possessive pronoun: `of mine`, `of yours`, `of his`, `of hers`, `of ours`, `of theirs`
- with a person's name or noun: `of Anna's`, `of my brother's`
- the same after `this`, `that`, `some`, `any`, `no` and numbers: `that car of yours`, `two friends of ours`
- possessive pronouns, never object pronouns or possessive adjectives after `of`
- no article and possessive adjective together: no `a my`, `the my`
- plural: `friends of mine`, `some colleagues of his`

**When it applies**
- Introducing one person or thing from a group: a friend, a cousin, a colleague, a song
- Comments with feeling after `this` / `that`: `that dog of theirs`
- After numbers and `some`, `any`

**When it does NOT apply** — For a specific, known person, use a possessive adjective (`my friend`) or the noun with 's (`Anna's sister`). Test: one of several and new to the listener? → `a ... of mine`. The one the listener already knows? → `my` + noun.

**Typical mistakes**
- `a my friend`: article + possessive adjective, copied word for word
- `one my friend`: the correct choices are `a friend of mine` or `one of my friends`
- `of me`, `of them`: object pronoun instead of possessive pronoun
- `of my`, `of your` at the end with no noun
- `two my students`, `any your friend`: number or determiner + possessive adjective

**Register and usage** — Neutral and frequent in conversation and stories.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `a photo of him` (showing him) differs from `a photo of his` (owned by him)
rules.llmDescription: Double possessive a, this, some, two + noun + of + mine, yours, theirs or noun's: errors a my friend, one my friend, of me, of them.

rules.title: The second conditional
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You use it to imagine things, dream, and give advice like "If I were you...".

**In simple words** — `If` + past, `would` + verb: `If I had a million, I would travel`. It talks about unreal or unlikely situations now.

**The idea** — The second conditional speaks about situations that are unreal, imaginary or very unlikely now. The speaker pictures a different world and says what would happen in it. The past form signals distance from reality, not past time.

**The form**
- `if` + past simple, `would` + base verb: `if I had`, `I would buy`
- With `be`, `were` is used for all persons in careful English: `if I were you`; `was` is common in speech
- Negative: `wouldn't` + base verb; `if` + `didn't` + base verb
- Question: `What would you do if you ...?`; `Would you ... if ...?`
- Other results: `could` or `might` instead of `would`
- Never use `would` in the `if` clause (`if I would have`)

**When it applies**
- Imaginary present or future situations: signal words `if I were`, `imagine`, `suppose`
- Giving advice: `if I were you`
- Unlikely future events: `if I won the lottery`

**When it does NOT apply** — For a real, possible future use the first conditional (`if` + present, `will`); for an imaginary past use the third conditional (`if` + past perfect). Test: if the situation is unreal or unlikely now or in the future, use the past after `if` and `would` in the result.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `would` in the `if` clause, because the result clause has it
- Using the present simple after `if`, which makes the situation real
- Using `will` in the result
- Using `is/was` instead of `were` in formal advice such as `if I were you`

**Register and usage** — `if I were you` is the fixed advice formula; both `was` and `were` occur in speech.
rules.llmDescription: Second conditional if plus past simple with would in the result for unreal present or future: would in the if clause, present after if, will in the result.

rules.title: The third conditional
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — You use it to express regret, relief or criticism about the past.

**In simple words** — `If` + past perfect, `would have` + participle: `If I had studied, I would have passed`. It is about something that did not happen.

**The idea** — The third conditional looks back at the past and imagines a different result. The speaker talks about something that did not happen and what would have followed. It is the form of regret, criticism and relief.

**The form**
- `if` + past perfect, `would have` + past participle: `had known`, `would have told`
- Contracted: `I'd have`, `hadn't`, `wouldn't have`
- Negative: `hadn't` + participle in the `if` part; `wouldn't have` + participle in the result
- Question: `What would you have done if ...?`
- Other results: `could have`, `might have` + participle
- Never use `would have` in the `if` clause (`if you would have asked`)

**When it applies**
- Unreal past situations: signal words `if only`, `I wish`, `too late`, `at that time`
- Regrets and criticism of past choices
- Explaining what a different event would have changed

**When it does NOT apply** — For an unreal present use the second conditional; for a possible future use the first. Test: if you look back at something that did not happen and can no longer change, use the past perfect after `if` and `would have` in the result.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `would have` in both clauses, because the result form is copied into the `if` clause
- Using the simple past after `if`, which sounds like the second conditional
- Using the base form or past form instead of the participle in the result (`would told`, `would have went`)
- Using `will have` in the result

**Register and usage** — In speech `'d` stands for both `had` and `would`; this is common and normal.
rules.llmDescription: Third conditional if plus past perfect with would have plus participle for unreal past situations: would have after if, simple past after if, missing have or participle in the result.
