rules.title: Who or whom
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — It matters mainly in formal writing, and using `whom` wrongly is a bigger risk than avoiding it.

**In simple words** — `whom` is the formal object form: `To whom did you speak?` In everyday speech `who` is normal.

**The idea** — `Whom` is the object form of `who`, just as `him` is the object form of `he`. In everyday English `who` is used for objects too, so the choice matters mainly in formal writing. The real trap is the opposite: learners use `whom` because it sounds formal, even where the word is the subject of a verb.

**The form**
- Subject of the verb: `who` + verb — `who called`, `the woman who lives`
- Object in formal style: `whom` + its own subject + verb — `whom did you invite`, `the man whom she married`
- Quick test: answer with `he` or `him`; `he` → `who`, `him` → `whom`
- Inserted clause: `who I think is`, `who they say was`; the inserted `I think` does not change the role
- `whoever` is the subject of its own clause, `whomever` its object, whatever comes before: `to whoever needs it`
- Subject questions: `Who` + verb, no `did`; object questions: `Who/Whom` + `did` + subject + verb
- Embedded questions follow the same test: `know who is coming`

**When it applies**
- Formal letters, reports, academic and legal writing
- Questions and relative clauses where `whom` is tempting: `Who/Whom do you think ...?`, `the person who/whom ...`
- Free relatives with `whoever` and `whomever`

**When it does NOT apply** — The rule for a preposition before `whom` and `which` (`to whom`, `most of whom`) deals with preposition placement; this rule decides between `who` and `whom` by the word's role in its own clause. Test: find the verb that follows; if `who/whom` is its subject, use `who`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `whom` as a subject (`whom is responsible`), because it sounds more correct
- Using `whom` before an inserted `I think` or `they say`: the word is still the subject of the next verb
- Choosing `whomever` after a preposition when it is the subject of the clause (`to whomever wants it`)
- Using `whom` in embedded questions where it is the subject (`wonder whom sent`)

**Register and usage** — `Whom` is formal; in speech `who` is normal for objects, but `whom` for a subject is wrong in every register.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- Fixed formal phrases keep `whom`: `To whom it may concern`, `with whom`, `of whom`
rules.llmDescription: Who or whom by role in its clause: whom as subject, whom before inserted I think or they say, whomever as subject. Not preposition placement before whom.

rules.title: Should after emotional reactions
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — It is formal and rare, found in careful writing.

**In simple words** — After words of surprise or regret: `It's strange that he should say that`, `I'm surprised that she should ask`.

**The idea** — After words of surprise, regret or judgement, formal English can put `should` into the `that`-clause. This `should` has nothing to do with duty: it presents the event as an idea the speaker reacts to, which sounds more distant and emphatic than a plain tense.

**The form**
- `It is` + adjective or noun + `that` + subject + `should` + bare verb: `strange that she should say`
- Past event: `should have` + past participle: `odd that he should have left`
- Passive: `should be` + participle: `should be invited`
- Negative: `should not` + bare verb, `should not have` + participle; `not` goes after `should`
- The same form for every person: no `-s`, no `to`, no past form after `should`
- Questions of protest: `Why should` + subject + bare verb
- Alternative: an ordinary tense (`that she says`, `that she said`), never a mixture of both

**When it applies**
- After `strange`, `odd`, `surprising`, `funny`, `natural`, `understandable`, `typical`, `ironic`
- After nouns `a pity`, `a shame`, `no wonder`; after `I'm surprised/sorry that`
- Fixed phrases: `funny you should mention`, `why should I care`

**When it does NOT apply** — `Should` for advice gives a recommendation, and the mandative subjunctive follows demands such as `suggest`, `insist`. Test: if the main clause expresses a feeling about an event, use this `should` or a plain tense; if it demands or proposes, use the mandative pattern; if it advises, use advice `should`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Adding `to` after `should` (`should to ignore`), as after `ought`
- Adding `-s`, `-ing` or a past form after `should`, because the subject or time seems to require it
- Writing `should has` or `should had` instead of `should have`
- Putting `not` after the main verb (`should be not invited`)
- Using bare `should` + past form for a past event instead of `should have` + participle

**Register and usage** — Formal and mainly British; American English often prefers a plain tense, but the `should` forms above are correct in both.
rules.llmDescription: Putative should after it's strange, odd, a pity, natural that, why should: wrong form after should, should has, misplaced not. Not advice should or mandative subjunctive.

rules.title: All the and none the with comparatives
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — It is a rare but natural way to say "even more because of that".

**In simple words** — `all the better` = even better because of that. `none the wiser` = no wiser in spite of it.

**The idea** — `All the` + comparative means 'even more, because of a particular reason': the reason makes the quality stronger. `None the` + comparative means 'not at all more': nothing changed despite what happened. The `the` here is an old word meaning 'by that much', so it cannot be dropped.

**The form**
- `all the` + comparative, often + `for` + noun or `because` + clause: `all the better for it`, `all the more important because`
- `none the` + comparative: `none the wiser`, `none the worse for`
- `so much the` + comparative: `so much the better`, `so much the worse`
- `all the more reason` + to-infinitive or `for` + noun
- The comparative is marked once: `-er` or `more`, never both; irregular `better`, `worse`
- The reason follows with `for` or `because`, never `than`
- `none` is already negative: no `not` in the same clause; the neutral negative is `not any the` + comparative
- Questions use `any the`: `any the wiser?`

**When it applies**
- Explaining what strengthens a quality: signal words `for it`, `because`, `since`, `given`
- Saying that something changed nothing: `none the wiser`, `none the worse`
- Welcoming or regretting a result: `so much the better`

**When it does NOT apply** — The rule for linked comparatives (`the more ... the better`) has two mirrored halves; this pattern has one comparative strengthened by a reason. Test: two `the` + comparative halves → the linked pattern; one comparative + reason → this pattern.

**Typical mistakes**
- Dropping `the` (`all more difficult`, `none wiser`)
- Using a superlative (`all the most painful`)
- Marking the comparative twice (`all the more angrier`)
- Giving the reason with `than` instead of `for` or `because`
- Adding `not` to `none the`, which makes a double negative
- Replacing `none` with `nothing` or `no`

**Register and usage** — Mostly written and formal; `none the wiser` and `so much the better` are also common in speech.
rules.llmDescription: All the, none the, so much the plus comparative: missing the, superlative, double comparative, than instead of for or because, not with none. Not the more ... the more.

rules.title: Lest and for fear that
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — It is formal, old-fashioned and rare; you will mostly recognise it in literature.

**In simple words** — `Take notes lest you forget` = so that you don't forget.

**The idea** — `Lest`, `for fear that` and `for fear of` express negative purpose: someone acts to prevent a feared result. `Lest` already means 'so that ... not', so the clause after it is positive in form and its verb is a subjunctive.

**The form**
- `lest` + subject + bare verb, the same for all persons: `lest he forget`
- `lest` + subject + `should` + bare verb: `lest anyone should think`
- Passive: `lest` + subject + `be` + past participle: `lest it be lost`
- `for fear that` + subject + `might`, `would` or `should` + bare verb after a past main verb; `may` or `will` after a present one
- `for fear of` + noun or `-ing`: `for fear of waking`, `for fear of being seen`
- No `not` after `lest` unless the opposite is meant; no `will`, `-s` or past form after `lest`
- `for fear of` never takes a full clause; `for fear that` never takes an `-ing` form
- After words of fear: `afraid lest`, `worried lest` + the same subjunctive

**When it applies**
- Formal, literary, religious and legal writing
- Precautions and warnings: signal words `quietly`, `carefully`, `hid`, `locked`, `kept still`

**When it does NOT apply** — The purpose rule (`so that`, `in order to`) is for a positive aim; `so that ... not` is the neutral negative equivalent of `lest`. `In case` + present is a precaution for an event that may happen anyway. Test: if you can rephrase with `so that ... not`, `lest` or `for fear that` fits; if the aim is positive, use the purpose rule.

**Typical mistakes**
- Adding `not` or `don't` after `lest`, which doubles the negative
- Using `-s`, a past form or `will` after `lest`, copied from ordinary clauses
- Putting a full clause after `for fear of` or an `-ing` form after `for fear that`
- Keeping `will` after `for fear that` when the main verb is past

**Register and usage** — `Lest` is very formal or literary; `for fear of` is common in writing; in speech use `so that ... not` or `in case`.
rules.llmDescription: Negative purpose: lest plus bare verb, for fear that plus modal, for fear of plus -ing; not, -s or will after lest, clause after for fear of. Not so that.

examples.correct: He spoke quietly lest he wake the baby.
examples.note: Use the bare verb after lest.

examples.wrong: We must act now lest it will be too late.
examples.correct: We must act now lest it be too late.

examples.wrong: I kept still lest anyone should noticed me.
examples.correct: I kept still lest anyone should notice me.
examples.note: Use the bare verb after should.

examples.wrong: Don't leave the gate open lest the dog escapes.
examples.correct: Don't leave the gate open lest the dog escape.

examples.wrong: He didn't call for fear that she will say no.
examples.correct: He didn't call for fear that she would say no.
examples.note: After a past verb use would.

examples.wrong: Were you worried lest the old bridge collapsed?
examples.correct: Were you worried lest the old bridge collapse?
examples.note: Use the bare verb after lest.

examples.wrong: The documents were locked away lest they are stolen.
examples.correct: The documents were locked away lest they be stolen.
examples.note: Use be, not are, after lest.

rules.title: Many a with a singular noun
rules.description:
**Why learn it** — It is literary and rare; you will mostly recognise it.

**In simple words** — `Many a man has tried` = many men have tried. The noun and verb are singular.

**The idea** — `Many a` + singular noun means 'many', but it pictures the items one by one, which gives a literary, emphatic tone. Because the noun is singular, the verb is singular too, even though the meaning is plural.

**The form**
- `many a` + singular countable noun: `many a time`, `many a student`
- `many an` before a vowel sound: `many an hour`, `many an evening`
- An adjective can come in between: `many a long night`, `many a good man`
- Singular verb: `has`, `is`, `was`, `-s` in the present
- Pronouns referring back: singular `he/she/it`, or `their` in modern usage
- Literary fronting: `Many a time` + inverted or normal order
- Uncountable nouns need a unit: `many a piece of advice`
- Negatives and questions are not built with `many a`: use `not many` or `how many` + plural

**When it applies**
- Storytelling, speeches and proverbs: `many a true word is spoken in jest`, `many a slip`
- Emphasising repetition: `many a time`, `many a night`, `on many an occasion`

**When it does NOT apply** — The rule for `much`, `many` and `a lot of` uses plural nouns with plural verbs, and so does `a great many` or `a good many`. Test: if `a` or `an` comes straight after `many`, make the noun and the verb singular; otherwise make them plural.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using a plural noun after `many a` (`many a students`), because the meaning is plural
- Using a plural verb (`many a man have`), for the same reason
- Dropping the article (`many time`) and losing the fixed phrase
- Using `many a` with an uncountable noun (`many a advice`)
- Using `a` before a vowel sound (`many a hour`)
- Copying the singular into `a great many` (`a great many visitor`)

**Register and usage** — Rare and literary; common only in fixed phrases such as `many a time`. In neutral style use `many` + plural.
rules.llmDescription: Many a or many an plus singular noun and verb: plural noun or verb after many a, missing a, uncountable noun; a great many takes plural. Not plain many.

examples.wrong: Many a student have failed this exam.
examples.correct: Many a student has failed this exam.
examples.note: Many a takes a singular verb.

examples.wrong: I've walked this road many a times.
examples.correct: I've walked this road many a time.
examples.note: Use a singular noun after many a.

examples.wrong: Many a good men has tried and failed.
examples.correct: Many a good man has tried and failed.
examples.note: Use a singular noun after many a.

examples.wrong: She spent many a hour in the library.
examples.correct: She spent many an hour in the library.
examples.note: Use an before a vowel sound.

examples.wrong: Many a parents worries about screen time.
examples.correct: Many a parent worries about screen time.
examples.note: Use a singular noun after many a.

examples.wrong: A great many visitor come here every summer.
examples.correct: A great many visitors come here every summer.
examples.note: A great many takes a plural noun.

examples.wrong: Many time I wondered what they meant.
examples.correct: Many a time I wondered what they meant.

examples.wrong: Many a advice was ignored by the board.
examples.correct: Many a piece of advice was ignored by the board.
examples.note: Advice is uncountable; use a piece of.

examples.wrong: Many a promise were broken that year.
examples.correct: Many a promise was broken that year.
examples.note: Many a takes a singular verb.

examples.wrong: Many a true words is spoken in jest.
examples.correct: Many a true word is spoken in jest.
examples.note: Use a singular noun after many a.
